en: The King said:
All the Manvantaras have been described by you and heard by me,
as well as the heroic deeds performed therein by Hari, whose valor is infinite.
That royal sage named Satyavrata, the lord of Draviḍa,
who obtained knowledge by serving the Supreme Person at the end of the past kalpa—
he indeed became Manu, the son of Vivasvat; so it has been heard.
From you, his sons, the kings headed by Ikṣvāku, have been described.
O Brahmin, O illustrious one, please proclaim their lineage separately, as well as the histories of their dynasties, for we are constantly desirous of hearing them.
"Tell us of the heroic exploits of all those of meritorious fame— those who were in the past, those who will be in the future, and those who exist in the present.
Śrī Sūta said:
Thus questioned by King Parīkṣit in the assembly of those who discourse on Brahman,
the blessed Śuka, the knower of the supreme dharma, spoke. Śrī Śuka said:
O scorcher of enemies, listen to the lineage of Manu in its full extent;
it cannot be described in detail even in hundreds of years.
He who is the Supreme Person, the Self of all beings, both high and low—
At the end of the kalpa, He alone existed as this entire universe, and nothing else whatsoever;
from His navel there arose a golden lotus bud,
and within it, O great king, was born the self-born one with four faces.
From his mind, Marīci was born; from him, Kaśyapa was born of Dākṣāyaṇī. From him, Vivasvān became the son of Aditi.
From him, O descendant of Bharata, Manu Śrāddhadeva was born of Saṃjñā.
The self-possessed and powerful king begot ten sons upon Śraddhā:
Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Śaryāti, Diṣṭa, Dhṛṣṭa, Karūṣaka,
Nariṣyanta, Pṛṣadhra, Nabhaga, and Kavi.
Formerly, it is said, when Manu was childless, the powerful and venerable Vasiṣṭha performed a sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa for the sake of progeny;
there, Manu’s wife Śraddhā requested the Hotṛ priest.
Having approached for the sake of his daughter and prostrated himself, the Hotṛ priest, who had observed the milk-vow,
was dispatched by the Adhvaryu; with a concentrated mind,
that twice-born one moved about while mentally uttering the *vaṣaṭ* call over the offered oblation.
Due to that transgression of the Hotṛ priest, she became a maiden named Ilā.
Beholding her, Manu, with a mind not at all pleased, said to his preceptor:
"O Blessed One, what is this that has occurred among you who are teachers of the Veda?"
"What a terrible reversal! May such a distortion of Brahman never occur.
You are knowers of Brahman, disciplined, and your sins have been burnt away by austerity;
how could there be such a perversion of resolve, like falsehood among the gods?"

Having heard those words of his and perceiving the transgression of the *hotṛ* priest, the Blessed One, the Great-Grandfather, spoke to the son of the Sun: "This discrepancy in your resolve is due to the *hotṛ*'s deviation."
"Nevertheless, by my own power, I shall grant you the blessing of good offspring.
O King, having thus resolved, the illustrious Lord, of great fame,
offered praise to the Primeval Person out of a desire for Ilā to attain manhood.
Being pleased with him, the blessed Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, granted him a boon of his choice; by that, O bull among men, Ilā became Sudyumna.
Once, O great king, while he was wandering in the forest on a hunt, he—
Accompanied by a few ministers, the hero mounted a Saindhava horse,
took up a splendid bow and most wonderful arrows,
and clad in armor, followed the deer toward the northern direction.
He entered the Sukumāra forest at the foot of Mount Meru,
where the Blessed Lord Śarva dwells, sporting with Umā.
As soon as he had entered it, Sudyumna, the slayer of enemy heroes, [was transformed].
O King, he saw himself as a woman and his horse as a mare; likewise, all his followers, seeing this reversal of their own genders,
became despondent as they looked at one another.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, how is this land endowed with such qualities, and by whom was it created?
Explain this question to us, for our curiosity is great."
Śrī Śuka said:
Once, certain sages of firm vows arrived there to behold Giriśa,
illuminating the quarters with a light that dispelled all darkness.
Seeing them, the goddess Ambikā, being naked, was deeply ashamed;
rising from her husband's lap, she quickly adjusted her lower garment.
The sages, too, beheld the union of the two as they were sporting.
Having turned back from there, they proceeded to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Regarding this, the Blessed One spoke out of a desire to please his beloved:
"Whoever should enter this place shall indeed become a woman."
From that time on, men indeed avoided that forest;
she, accompanied by her attendants, wandered from forest to forest.
Then, as that most excellent of women was wandering near a hermitage—
Seeing her surrounded by women, the wise Lord Budha desired her;
she too, the fair-browed one, desired him as her husband, the son of Soma’s king.
He begot upon her a son, Purūravas.
Thus, having attained womanhood, King Sudyumna, the son of Manu, remembered his family preceptor Vasiṣṭha; so we have heard. Seeing his condition, the sage was deeply pained with compassion.
Sudyumna, seeking manhood, approached Śaṅkara;
pleased with him, the Blessed One,
bringing him his desired boon and making his own word true, spoke thus, O lord of the people.

"For one month that descendant of your lineage shall be a man, and for one month he shall be a woman; by this arrangement, Sudyumna shall enjoy his desire and protect the earth. Having obtained his desired masculinity through this arrangement by the grace of his preceptor, [he ruled].
He protected the world, yet the subjects did not rejoice in him.
O King, he had three sons— Utkala, Gaya, and Vimala—
who became kings of the southern region and were devoted to righteousness.
Then, when the time had matured, the lord and ruler of Pratiṣṭhāna,
having entrusted the earth to his son Purūravas, departed for the forest.
Śrī Śuka said:
When Sudyumna had thus departed, Manu Vaivasvata,
desiring a son, performed austerities for a hundred years on the banks of the Yamunā. Thereafter, for the sake of offspring, Manu worshipped the Lord Hari, the Supreme Deity.
He obtained ten sons, born before Ikṣvāku, who were like himself.
Pṛṣadhra, however, the son of Manu, was appointed as a cowherd by his elder brother;
observing the vow of the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), he diligently protected the cows during the night.
Once, while it was raining at night, a tiger entered the cow-pen.
The cows, who were lying down, rose up in fear and wandered about in the settlement.
A powerful tiger seized one; she, overcome by terror, cried out.
Hearing her cry, Pṛṣadhra pursued her;
taking up his sword with haste in the night when the host of stars had vanished, he—
mistaking her for a tiger— severed the head of Babhru without realizing who she was.
Then the tiger, its ears severed by the tip of the sword,
fled in great terror, shedding blood along the path; meanwhile,
Pṛṣadhra, the slayer of enemy heroes, thought the tiger had been killed.
When the night had dawned, the grieving king saw that Babhru had been killed.
His family preceptor cursed him for his intentional crime, saying:
"By this deed, you shall become a *kṣatrabandhu*, a *śūdra*."
Thus cursed by his preceptor, the hero, with palms joined in reverence, accepted [the command] and observed the vow dear to the sages, remaining celibate;
he fixed his mind upon Vāsudeva, the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, the Transcendent and Stainless.
Having attained single-minded devotion through bhakti, he was a friend to all beings,
impartial, liberated from attachment, tranquil in soul, with senses restrained, and free from possessions;
he sustained his own livelihood with whatever came to him by chance.
Having established the self within the Self, satisfied by knowledge and composed in meditation,
he wandered this earth with the appearance of one who is dull, blind, and deaf.
Living in such a manner, he went to the forest and saw a forest fire breaking out.
With his senses thus employed, the sage attained the Supreme Brahman;

the wise and youthful king, free from desire for sense-objects, having renounced the kingdom along with his kinsmen and established the Self-luminous Person within his heart, entered the forest in the prime of his youth and reached the highest state.
From Mānava were born the Karūṣas, who were of the kṣatriya caste;
they were the protectors of the northern region, devoted to Brahman, and lovers of dharma.
From Dhṛṣṭa arose the Dhārṣṭa kṣatriyas, who attained the state of Brahman on this earth.
The lineage of Nṛga consisted of Sumati, then Bhūtajyotis, and from him came Vasu.
From Vasu was born Pratīka; his son was Oghavān, and Oghavān’s father was [Vasu]. He had a daughter named Oghavatī, whom Sudarśana married.
Citrasena was born from Nariṣyanta; his son was Ṛkṣa.
His son was Mīḍhvān, from whom Pūrṇa was born, and Indrasena was his son.
Vītihotra was born from Indrasena, and Satyaśravas was his son.
His son was Uruśravas, from whom Devadatta was born. From him was born the venerable Agniveśya, who was the Lord Agni himself; he was the great sage widely known as Kānīna Jātūkarṇya.
From him, O King, was born the Brahmin lineage of Āgniveśyāyana;
this is declared to be the lineage of Nariṣyanta. Now hear the lineage of Diṣṭa. Nābhāga was another son of Diṣṭa who, by his actions, attained the status of a Vaiśya.
Bhalandana was his son; from Bhalandana came Vatsaprīti.
The son of Vatsaprīti was Prāṃśu, and they know his son to be Pramati. From Pramati came Khanitra, and from him were born Cākṣuṣa and Viviṃśati.
The son of Viviṃśati was Rambha; his son was the righteous Khanīnetra.
O King, Karandhama was the son of that king.
His son was Avīkṣita, whose son was the universal emperor Marutta.
Saṃvarta, the son of Aṅgiras and a great yogi, performed the sacrifice for Marutta; indeed, no other sacrifice was ever like it. Everything that was beautiful there was made entirely of gold.
Indra was intoxicated by the soma, and the twice-born were gratified by the sacrificial fees;
the Maruts were the servers, and the Viśvedevas were the members of the assembly.
Marutta’s son was Dama, who increased his father’s kingdom.
Sudhṛti was born as his son; Nara was the son of Sudhṛti. His son was Kevala, from whom came Dhundhumān, and from him Vegavān.
Budha was his son, whose son was the lord of the earth, Tṛṇabindu.
The divine lady Alambuṣā, the most excellent of Apsarases, devoted herself to him, who was an abode of qualities worthy of worship;
from her were born sons and a daughter, Ilavilā,
as well as Dhanada, whom Viśravas begot as his son.
The Ṛṣi, the lord of yoga, bestowed supreme knowledge upon his father.
Viśāla, Śūnyabandhu, and Dhūmraketu were his sons;
King Viśāla was the founder of the lineage who established the city of Vaiśālī.
His son was Hemacandra, and his son was Dhūmrākṣa.
From his son Saṃyama was born Kṛśāśva, who was the son of Sahadeva. From Kṛśāśva was born Somadatta, who [propitiated] Indra with horse-sacrifices.
Having worshipped Puruṣa, they attained the supreme goal resorted to by the masters of yoga.
Sumati, the son of Somadatta, was Janamejaya;
these were the kings of Vaiśālī, the upholders of the fame of Tṛṇabindu.
Śrī Śuka said:
King Śaryāti, the son of Manu, was a sovereign most devoted to Brahman;
he was indeed the one who prescribed the second day of the sacrificial session of the Aṅgirases.
He had a lotus-eyed daughter named Sukanyā;
while wandering in the forest with her, he arrived at the hermitage of Cyavana.
There, surrounded by her companions, she was searching for trees in the forest.
Two lights were seen within the hole of an anthill like two fireflies;
impelled by fate, those boys, out of childish curiosity, pierced those lights with a thorn, and blood flowed out from them.
At that very moment, the soldiers' passage of feces and urine was obstructed.
Observing this, the royal sage was struck with wonder and said to his men:
"Have you not committed some ill deed against the descendant of Bhṛgu?"
"Clearly, someone has committed an offense against our hermitage.
Frightened, Sukanyā said to her father, "I have done something;
not knowing there were two lights, they were indeed pierced by me with a thorn."
Having heard those words of his daughter, Śaryāti became filled with trepidation;
he gradually propitiated the sage who was hidden within the anthill.
Having understood his intention, the king gave his daughter to the sage.
Released from his hardships, he took leave of him and departed for his city with a composed mind.
Having obtained Cyavana as her husband, though he was extremely irascible,
Sukanyā pleased him by understanding his heart and through constant, vigilant service.
Then, after some time had passed, the two Nāsatyas came to his hermitage; having honored them, he said, "O Lords, grant me my youth,
for I shall take up the soma at your sacrifice, even though you both are drinkers of no soma."
"Let my age and form be made such as is desired by young women.
"So be it," the two excellent physicians replied, greeting the brahmin,
and said, "May you immerse yourself in this lake created by the Siddhas."
Thus addressed, his body seized by old age, covered with visible veins,
and marked by wrinkles and grey hair, he was made to enter a lake by the two Aśvins;
from it there arose three men who were free from fat and dear to women.
Wearing lotus garlands, adorned with earrings, identical in form,
and well-dressed— seeing them, who were of equal beauty and possessed the luster of the sun,
that virtuous woman of noble hips, not recognizing her husband, sought refuge with the two Aśvins.
Having shown themselves to her, being satisfied by her devotion to her husband,
they took leave of the sage and departed for heaven in a celestial chariot. Then Śaryāti, intending to perform a sacrifice, went to the hermitage of Cyavana.

Beside his daughter, he saw a man with the splendor of the sun. The king, having failed to offer blessings to his daughter who had performed her salutation at his feet, spoke to her as if his mind were not particularly pleased.
"What is this you intend to do? You have deceived your husband, that sage honored by the world!

Since you have abandoned him, who was seized by old age and esteemed as untruthful, you now devote yourself to this traveler, a paramour. "How has your mind become so perverted, O you born of a noble family—this is indeed a disgrace to your lineage!"
"Since you, shameless as you are, support a paramour, you lead the family of your father and that of your husband into the lowest darkness.
To her father who was speaking thus, she, smiling with a pure smile, replied:
"O dear father, this descendant of Bhṛgu is your son-in-law."
He related all of that—the attainment of youth and beauty—to his father.
Astonished and supremely delighted, the father embraced his daughter. While performing a sacrifice for the hero with Soma, he drew the soma-graha cup.
Although Cyavana was not the son of Aśvinī, by his own spiritual power he seized the thunderbolt to strike him; for his anger was instantly provoked by indignation.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu paralyzed the arm of Indra together with the thunderbolt.
Then they all authorized the drinking of Soma for the Aśvins, saying, "They are physicians," even though they had previously been excluded from the Soma offering.
There were three [sons]: Uttānabarhis, Ānarta, and Bhūriṣeṇa.

Śaryāti had sons; from Ānarta was born Revata. Having constructed the city of Kuśasthalī within the ocean, he, the subduer of enemies, resided there and enjoyed the territories of Ānarta and other regions.
To him were born a hundred sons, of whom Kakudmin was the eldest and most excellent.
Kakudmin, taking his daughter Revatī with him,
went to the presence of the Lord in order to inquire about a suitable bridegroom for his daughter in the open realm of Brahmā.

While the Gandharva music continued, he, finding no opportunity for a moment, waited; at its conclusion, having bowed down, he announced his own intention. Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Brahmā laughed and spoke to him.
"O King, alas! Those who were held within your heart have been swept away by Time;
we no longer hear even the names of their lineages, nor of their sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons. Time has passed, comprising twenty-seven cycles of the four ages."
Therefore, O King, go; Baladeva, the portion of the God of gods and possessed of great strength, is here.
Give this jewel of a maiden to that jewel among men, for the Lord, the creator of all beings, has descended to remove the burden of the earth.
"Having descended with a portion of himself, he whose hearing and chanting are meritorious"—
having been thus instructed, the king, after bowing to the Unborn One (Brahmā), returned to his own city,
where [the demons] had been abandoned by his brothers who were stationed in various directions out of fear of the Puṇyajanas.
Having given his daughter of faultless limbs to the powerful Balarāma,
the king went to the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa at Badarī to perform austerities.

"O my son, your noble elders have broken your fast; do not disregard them. O wise one, these highly intelligent Aṅgirasas are performing a sacrificial session today;
having approached every sixth day, they become bewildered in their ritual duties."

"Recite for them the two Vaiśvadeva hymns of the Great-Souled One; they, departing for heaven, will give you their own remaining wealth from the sacrificial session. Go to them," he said, and he did exactly as instructed.
Having given that which remained from their sacrificial session to him, they went to heaven. Then,
as he was about to take possession of it, a certain man with a dark complexion approached from the north and said, "This property belongs to me."
"Then the man [Nimi] would have thought, 'This has been given to me by the sages';
thus there would have been a question for us regarding your father, just as he questioned his own father.
At one time, all the remnants of the sacrificial ground were present among the sages."
They indeed assigned a share to Rudra, for that god deserves everything.
Nābhāga bowed before him and said, "O Lord, this dwelling place is surely yours," he said to me, O Brahmin; I propitiate you with my head bowed low.
"Since your father spoke of dharma and you yourself speak the truth,
I grant you, who perceive the mantras, knowledge of the eternal Brahman. Accept this wealth given as the remainder of my sacrifice."
Having spoken thus, the Lord Rudra, who is devoted to righteousness, vanished.
He who, being well-composed, should remember this in the morning and in the evening,
becomes a wise poet, a knower of mantras, and likewise attains his own true goal.
From Nābhāga was born Ambarīṣa, a great devotee of the Lord and a man of virtuous deeds;
even the curse of a brahmin, which elsewhere is never thwarted, did not touch him.
Śrī Rājā said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about that wise royal sage,
against whom the insurmountable curse of Brahmā proved powerless once he was released.
Śrī Śuka said:
The highly fortunate Ambarīṣa, having obtained the earth with its seven islands, as well as imperishable prosperity and incomparable power on this world,
considered all of that— which is so difficult for men to attain— to be no more than a dream.

The wise man who has attained supreme devotion toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, toward his devotees, and toward the virtuous— by means of which he regards this entire universe as being like a clod of earth— enters that darkness which is the extinction of all manifestation.
He fixed his mind upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa; his speech was employed in describing the qualities of Vaikuṇṭha;

his hands were engaged in the cleaning of Hari’s temple and other such tasks; he applied his ears to the arising of the sacred narrations of Acyuta; his eyes were directed toward the sight of the temples containing the icons of Mukunda; and his body found its union with the touch of the limbs of His servants.
May my sense of smell be devoted to the fragrance of the lotus feet of Him whose feet are the source of the glorious *tulasī*; may my tongue be fixed upon what is offered to Him;
may my feet be intent on treading the sacred sites of Hari; may my head be engaged in bowing at the feet of Hṛṣīkeśa;
and may my desire be for service, not for the gratification of selfish desires, so that my love finds its refuge in those who praise the Lord of Excellent Renown (*uttamaśloka*).

Thus, always performing the entire range of his ritual duties for the Supreme Lord Adhokṣaja, who is the object of sacrifice and the Self of all, and being instructed by Brahmins devoted to Him, he ruled this earth. He worshipped the Lord, the object of sacrifice, with horse sacrifices in which the limbs of the rites were enriched by vast wealth and sacrificial fees.
Then, accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, Asita, Gautama, and others, he went along the Dhanvā river against the current to the Sarasvatī;
at whose sacrifices the gods, the members of the assembly,
and the officiating priests were seen to be identical in form— unblinking and well-attired.
He for whom heaven— so dear to the immortals— is not sought by men who listen to and sing of the deeds of the One of Supreme Renown (Uttamaśloka),
and for whom the desires nurtured by sovereign rule increase; [he alone attains the goal].
Even for the perfected ones (*siddhas*), Mukunda is not easily perceived within the heart.
Thus, O King, by means of the yoga of devotion joined with austerity,
and by pleasing Hari through his own duty, he gradually abandoned all desires.
He turned his mind away from his houses, wives, sons, kinsmen, and possessions such as excellent elephants, chariots, and horses;
he lost interest in inexhaustible jewels, ornaments, garments, and the like, and in his endless treasuries. To him, Hari gave the discus, which brings fear to his enemies.
Delighted by the spirit of his exclusive devotion, the heroic king, desiring to fulfill his protection of his devotees,
observed the Dvādaśī vow for one year together with his queen, who shared his same character.

At the conclusion of his vow, in the month of Kārtika, having fasted for three nights and bathed in the Kālindī, he once worshipped Hari in Madhuvana according to the ritual of the great consecration, with all articles of excellence provided.

Having consecrated Keśava with garments, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, he worshipped Him with a heart entirely absorbed in Him; and he also reverently honored the highly fortunate brāhmaṇas who had attained their goals.

He sent six hundred million cows to the virtuous brāhmaṇas in their homes— cows with golden horns and silver hooves, beautifully adorned with cloths, and endowed with excellent milk, character, age, appearance, calves, and trappings.
Having first fed the twice-born with sweet food of the highest quality,
and being permitted by them once their desires were fulfilled, he prepared to break his fast;
at that time, the venerable Durvāsas himself appeared as his guest.
The king honored that guest with rising from his seat, offering a seat, and respectful salutation;
having approached the guest's feet, he requested him to partake of food.
Having welcomed that request, the guest went to attend to his necessary duties.
Meditating deeply, he immersed himself in the auspicious waters of the Kālindī;
when half a muhūrta remained of the twelfth day before the breaking of the fast,
that knower of dharma reflected upon the dilemma regarding his religious duty in the company of the twice-born.
"There is a fault in transgressing against a brāhmaṇa, yet there is a greater fault in not breaking my fast on the twelfth day.
Whatever I do that may be good for me, or whatever unrighteousness might touch me, let it be so;
I shall instead perform the breaking of my vow with water alone."

"The Brahmins say that drinking water is neither eating nor not eating. Having thus sipped water and meditated upon Acyuta in his mind, O best of the Kurus, that royal sage perceived only the arrival of the twice-born.
Durvāsas, having returned from the banks of the Yamunā after attending to his necessary duties, was greeted with joy by the king; however, through his intelligence, he perceived the king's intention.
With his limbs trembling in wrath and his face contorted by a frown, he spoke.
And being exceedingly hungry, he spoke to him who stood with palms joined in reverence:
"Alas! Behold the transgression of dharma by this cruel man, intoxicated by prosperity—Viṣṇu’s devotee, yet one who considers himself the Lord."
"Since he invited me, a guest who had arrived, with the rites of hospitality,
yet ate without first giving [me anything], I shall immediately show him the fruit of that act.
Speaking thus, inflamed by rage, he tore out his matted hair.

By her, he created for him a *kṛtyā* resembling the fire of cosmic destruction. Seeing her rushing toward him, blazing, with a sword in hand, making the earth tremble under her feet, the king did not waver from his position.
The discus, previously directed by the high-souled Puruṣa for the protection of his servant, consumed that magical spell (kṛtyā) just as fire consumes an angry serpent;
seeing it rushing toward him and perceiving its own effort to be fruitless, [the demon fled].
Terrified, Durvāsas fled in all directions seeking to save his life;
the Lord’s discus pursued him like a forest fire with rising flames chasing a snake.
Seeing it closely following him, the sage fled toward Mount Meru, desiring to enter a cave.
Having gone to the quarters, the sky, the earth, the subterranean cavities, the oceans, the worlds with their guardians, and even the third heaven, he ran hither and thither;
wherever he fled, he beheld the Sudarśana discus, which was unbearable to behold. Finding no protector anywhere, his mind perpetually terrified, he sought a place of refuge.
He approached the god Viriñca, the Creator, saying: "O Self-born One, protect me, whose splendor is unconquered!
Śrī Brahmā said:
"This entire universe, along with my own abode, shall [dissolve] at the conclusion of my sport, at the end of the period known as two parārdhas."
Indeed, by a mere contraction of his eyebrows, he who is Time itself intends to utterly consume us;
yet I, Bhava, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, and the foremost among the lords of progeny, the lords of beings, and the chiefs of the gods—
all of us, having submitted to his command, carry upon our heads that which is for the welfare of the world.
Refused by Viriñca and tormented by the discus of Viṣṇu,
Durvāsas sought refuge with Śarva, the dweller of Kailāsa.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
"O Father, we have no power over that Infinite One, in whom even other unmanifested sheaths of living beings exist;
at the proper time they come into being and cease to be, while thousands like us wander therein.
"I am Sanatkumāra, Nārada, and the venerable Aja."
Kapila, Apāntaratamas, Devala, Dharma, Āsuri, and others headed by Marīci— these lords of the Siddhas who have seen the further shore—
even we all do not understand His illusory power, being ourselves veiled by that very illusion.
"This weapon of that Lord of the Universe is indeed unbearable for us;
therefore, seek refuge in Him alone, for Hari will provide you with well-being.
Thereupon, Durvāsas, despairing, went to the abode of the Blessed One.

Residing in that realm called Vaikuṇṭha together with Śrī, the Abode of Fortune, he—being scorched by the fire of the invincible weapon and trembling all over—fell at the base of His feet and cried out:
"O Acyuta, O Infinite One, O Lord who grants what is desired! O Creator of the Universe, protect me, a sinner!"
"O Creator, since I did not know Your supreme majesty, I have committed an offense against You and Your beloved ones;
please ordain the atonement for it—for even a denizen of hell is liberated when Your name is uttered. The Blessed Lord said:

"O twice-born one, I am indeed dependent on my devotees, as if I were not independent; for my heart is captivated by saintly devotees, O lover of those who take refuge in devotion. I do not desire even my own self without these saintly devotees of mine."
O Brahman, for those whose ultimate goal is me and who possess eternal prosperity—
how could I bear to abandon them, who have renounced their wives, homes, sons, kinsmen, lives, and even this supreme wealth to take refuge in me?
The saintly ones, whose hearts are bound to me and who possess equal vision,
bring me under their control through devotion, just as virtuous wives do for a good husband.
Through service to Me, you have attained the fourfold goal beginning with residence in My own realm (sālokya).
Being fulfilled by service, they do not desire anything else, for that is corrupted by time;
the saintly are my heart, and I am the heart of the saintly.
They know nothing other than Me, nor do I know even the slightest thing apart from them.
"O Brahmin, I shall tell you the means; listen to it. For this very soul is the instrument of your own destruction; therefore, go toward him without delay.
The splendor discharged against the virtuous brings misfortune back upon the one who hurls it."

Austerity and sacred knowledge—both of these bring about the supreme good for Brahmins; yet, for one who is ill-behaved, they lead to the opposite result for the doer. O Brāhmaṇa, go now, may you be blessed, to the king who is the son of Nābhāga.
"Ask forgiveness from the illustrious one; then there will be peace.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus instructed by the Blessed One, Durvāsas, who had been tormented by the discus, [approached].
Approaching Ambarīṣa, he, distressed with grief, grasped his feet. Seeing his effort and feeling ashamed by the touch of his feet, he—
greatly tormented by compassion— praised that weapon of Hari.
Ambarīṣa said:
You are Agni, you are the Lord Sūrya, and you are Soma, the lord of the luminaries. You are the waters, you are the earth, the ether, and the wind; you are the subtle elements and the senses.
O Sudarśana, obeisances unto you, the thousand-spoked one, beloved of Acyuta!
O destroyer of all weapons, may there be well-being for the brāhmaṇa, O Lord of Sacrifice (Iḍaspate)!
You are dharma, you are nectar, you are truth; you are sacrifice, the enjoyer of all sacrifices.

You are the guardian of the worlds, the soul of all; you are the supreme virile splendor. Obeisance to You, the bridge of dharma for the entire world, the comet of destruction for the unrighteous asuras, the protector of the three worlds, possessed of pure luster, swift as thought, and the performer of wondrous deeds—I praise You.

By your splendor, which consists of righteousness, darkness has been withdrawn and light has appeared for the vision of the great-souled ones. O Lord of Speech, your majesty is difficult to surpass; this form of yours is both the existent and the non-existent, the transcendent and the immanent.
When you were indeed released by the Unstained One (Aja), O Invincible One, you entered the strength of the Daityas and Dānavas.
Chopping incessantly at the arms, belly, thighs, feet, head, and neck in battle, you shine resplendent;

O protector of the world, you have been appointed by the wielder of the mace (Balarāma) to destroy the wicked. Therefore, for the sake of this brāhmaṇa and for the sake of our family deity, grant him well-being; for that indeed is our favor.
If we have given gifts or performed sacrifices, or if our own duty has been well-performed,
and if our family is devoted to the Brahmins and the gods, then let this twice-born man be freed from his fever.
If the Blessed One, the sole refuge of all virtues, is pleased with us—
"By regarding all beings as his own self, let the twice-born become free from fever.
Śrī Śuka said:
"While the king was thus offering praise, the Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu..."
By the king's entreaty, the sage ceased burning the Brahmin on all sides;
Durvāsas, then released from the heat of the fire-missile, became well-disposed and,
bestowing supreme blessings, praised that lord of the earth.
Durvāsas said:
"O King, today I have witnessed the greatness of the servants of Ananta; for even though you are a transgressor, you desire my blessings."
What indeed is difficult for the virtuous to perform, or what is difficult for the great-souled to renounce,
by whom the Blessed Lord Hari, the bull among the Sātvatas, has been taken as their refuge?
Merely by hearing His name, a person becomes stainless.
What indeed remains for the servants of that Tīrthapada?
O King, I have been graced by you, whose nature is exceedingly compassionate,
since you have cast my sin behind you and protected my life.
The king, having refrained from food himself out of a desire for his [the sage's] return,
clasped his feet, propitiated him, and fed him. Having eaten that hospitality which was offered with honor and fulfilled all desires, he remained there.
His soul satisfied, he respectfully said to the king, "Please eat.
"I am pleased and I am graced by you, a true devotee of the Lord, through your sight, touch, conversation, and hospitality which has become my own spiritual nourishment."
The celestial women repeatedly sing of this pure deed of yours;
and this earth shall proclaim your most meritorious fame.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus praised the king, Durvāsas was fully satisfied;
he took his leave and departed through the sky for the causeless realm of Brahmā. A full year passed while he remained gone before he returned.
Desiring a vision of that sage, King Ambarīṣa subsisted on water alone.
After Durvāsas had departed, Ambarīṣa gathered what was most pure for the twice-born’s use;
having witnessed both the sage’s deliverance and his distress, he recognized his own prowess as well as the supreme power of others.

Thus endowed with manifold virtues, that king offered his devotion through various ritual acts to Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self and Brahman; by this he transcended the realms of Viriñci and went beyond even the hells.
Śrī Śuka said:

Then the wise Ambarīṣa, having entrusted the kingdom to his sons of similar character, entered the forest, fixing his mind upon Vāsudeva within himself, with the flow of the material qualities destroyed. This is the meritorious narrative of King Ambarīṣa.
Chanting and meditating upon it, one becomes a devotee of the Blessed Lord. Those who hear the life-story of the high-souled Ambarīṣa all attain liberation through devotion and by the grace of Viṣṇu.
Śrī Śuka said:
Virūpa, Ketumān, and Chambhu were the three sons of Ambarīṣa. From Virūpa was born Pṛṣadaśva, and his son was Rathītara.
Requested for the sake of progeny by Rathītara, who was childless, Aṅgiras begot upon his wife sons endowed with spiritual luster.
These, though born from the field [of another], are indeed remembered as Āṅgirasas once again.
The descendants of Rathītara were the most eminent of the twice-born, endowed with excellent lands.
From Kṣuva, however, was born a son named Ikṣvāku from his nostril;
his hundred sons, of whom Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍaka were the eldest, followed him.
O King, before them in Āryāvarta there were twenty-five kings; after them were three, and others in between and elsewhere.
Once, on the occasion of an *aṣṭakā* śrāddha, Ikṣvāku gave instructions to his son.
"Let pure meat be brought; Vikukṣi, go without delay!
Saying "So be it," that hero went to the forest, killed deer fit for the ritual, and being exhausted and hungry, he forgot his purpose and caught a hare.

He offered the remainder to his father, and by him, the teacher was urged to consecrate it; however, having learned of his son's deed, the teacher declared, "This is defiled and unfit for ritual use," O King.
Upon hearing what the teacher had said regarding his son's action, the king—

In anger, he banished from the country his son, who had abandoned the sacred injunctions. But that son, practicing yoga, engaged in conversation with a Brahmin who possessed the means of knowledge; having cast off his body, he attained through him that which is supreme.
When his father had passed away, Vikukṣi returned and, ruling this earth, worshipped Hari with sacrifices; he became renowned as Śaśāda. His son was Purañjaya, who was called Indravāha.

He was also called Kakutstha; now hear his names according to his deeds. There was a battle between the gods and the Dānavas, and the hero was chosen by the gods, who had been defeated by the Daityas, as their protector from the rear.
By the command of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the Lord and Soul of the universe, Indra became his great bull to serve as his vehicle. Thus equipped, he took up his divine bow and sharp arrows.
Being praised as he ascended, desiring to fight and standing upon the hump [of the bull],
nourished by the splendor of the high-souled Puruṣa Viṣṇu,
he besieged the city of the Daityas in the western direction along with the gods.
With them, he engaged in a tumultuous and hair-raising battle;
with broad-headed arrows, he dispatched the Daityas who rushed against him in combat to Yama. Facing the fall of his arrows, which were as fierce as the fire at the end of an eon—
Being struck down, the Daityas fled to their own abodes;
having conquered them, that royal sage— known by various names— delivered all the supreme wealth along with the women to the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra).
The son of Purañjaya was Anenās; his son was Pṛthu.
From him came Viśvagandhi, then Candra, and Yuvanāśva was his son. Śrāvasta was his son, by whom the city of Śrāvastī was built.
Bṛhadaśva was born from him, and from him Śrāvasti; then came Kuvalayāśvaka,
the powerful one who, surrounded by twenty-one thousand sons, slew the demon named Dhundhu for the sake of pleasing Uttaṅka.
He was known as Dhundhumāra, and his sons all perished by the fire from Dhundhu’s mouth; O descendant of Bharata, only three remained: Dṛḍhāśva, Kapilāśva, and Bhadrāśva.
Dṛḍhāśva’s son was Haryaśva, and Nikumbha is recorded as his son. Bahulāśva was the son of Nikumbha, and Kṛśāśva was his [Bahulāśva’s] son; then came Senajit.
Yuvanāśva was born from him, but being childless, he retired to the forest.
Distressed by his hundred wives, the compassionate sages, being well-composed, performed a sacrifice dedicated to Indra for him. At night, the king, overcome by thirst, entered that sacrificial hall.

Seeing those brahmins lying there, he himself drank the consecrated water. Upon waking and perceiving that the pitcher was empty of water, O Lord, they asked, "Whose deed is this? Who has drunk the *puṃsavana* water?"
Having learned that the king had indeed drunk [the poison] sent by the Lord,
they offered obeisances to the Lord, exclaiming, "Oh, how great is the power of destiny!
Then, when the time had arrived, [the child] burst forth from his right side.
The son of Yuvanāśva was born as a universal emperor (cakravartin). [His mother said:
"What will this boy drink? He cries out intensely for breast-milk.
[Indra replied: "Child, I shall nourish you; do not weep," and thus Indra gave him his forefinger.
His father did not die, by the grace of the brahmins and the gods;
then Yuvanāśva attained perfection right there through austerity. O dear one, Indra indeed gave him the name Trasaddasyu.
For it was from him that the robbers, Rāvaṇa and others, trembled in agitation;
then Yauvanāśva, the lord Māndhātā, a sovereign emperor,
alone ruled the earth consisting of seven islands by the power of Acyuta.
And he, a knower of the Self, performed sacrifices with rituals accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
for the sake of the God who consists of all gods, who is the self of all, and who transcends the senses;
[he offered] the material, the mantra, the ritual procedure, the sacrifice itself, as well as the sacrificer and the officiating priests.
Dharma, place, and time— all this is of the nature of Him.
As far as the sun rises and as far as it sets,
all that is called the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva.
Upon Bindumatī, the daughter of Śaśabindu, the king begot Purukutsa, Ambarīṣa, and Mucukunda, who was a yogi. Their fifty sisters chose Saubhari as their husband.
Immersed in the waters of the Yamunā, performing supreme austerity,
the brāhmaṇa saw the bliss of the king of fish as they engaged in sexual union; filled with desire, he requested a single daughter from the king.

He too said, "O Brahmin, let her be taken at her own choice (svayaṃvara) according to your desire. He reflected, "I am disliked by women; I am considered old, wrinkled, gray-haired, and trembling," and thus he replied.
"I shall thus fulfill the desire of the celestial women;
how much more so that of the lords of men?"— thus resolved,
the Lord entered the opulent inner apartments of the princesses, escorted by the gatekeeper.

Surrounded by those princesses, that excellent groom was chosen as one among fifty; however, because their minds were fixed solely on him, they cast aside their mutual friendship and a great quarrel arose over him, each saying, "He is suitable for me, not for you."

That master of the Rig Veda, by means of those women whose splendor of austerity was unsurpassed, dwelt in houses furnished with priceless furnishings, amidst various groves, pure-watered lakes, and fragrant forests;
provided with costly beds, seats, garments, ornaments, baths, ointments, food, and garlands.
He constantly took delight among well-adorned women and men, while the twice-born sang his praises and the bees offered their hymns.
Indeed, upon observing that state of domestic life, the lord of the seven islands was so struck with wonder that he abandoned even the pride associated with universal sovereignty.
Thus, though devoted to his home and enjoying various objects of sense through diverse pleasures, he was not satisfied,
just as fire is never satiated by small drops of clarified butter. Once, while sitting there, he contemplated the concealment of the Self from himself.
The teacher of the Bahvṛcas saw [the fish] arising from its contact with the fish; he cried out:

"Alas! Behold my ruin, a wretched man whose vows were characterized by truthfulness! Because of association with this water-dweller within the water, the *brahman* that I had long maintained has been cast away."
One who desires liberation should renounce attachment to those engaged in the vow of sexual union;
with all his being, he should not let his external senses wander,
but moving alone in solitude, he should fix his mind upon the infinite Lord.
If one should form an attachment to virtuous people who observe those same vows,
then even a single ascetic may, through association with fish in the water,
produce fifty, or even five thousand, offspring.
My mind, its intelligence stolen by the qualities of *māyā*, perceives objects as its true purpose; thus, with my desires for the duties of both worlds unfulfilled, I do not reach their end.
Living thus in the home, I eventually became detached and took up the vow of renunciation (*nyāsa*).
He went to the forest, and his wives, who regarded their husband as a deity, followed him there. Having performed severe penance until he attained self-realization,
that self-possessed man, together with the sacred fires, united himself with the Supreme Self.
O Great King, having observed their husband’s spiritual destination,
they followed him by his power, just as flames follow an extinguished fire.
Śrī Śuka said:
The most eminent son of Māndhātṛ was the one celebrated as Ambarīṣa;
his son was Yauvanāśva, who was instigated by his grandfather;
Hārīta was his son—these were the foremost descendants of Māndhātṛ.
Narmadā was given to Purukutsa by his brothers, the serpents. Led by her, who was dispatched by the lord of the snakes, he went to Rasātala.
There, wielding the power of Viṣṇu, he slew the Gandharvas who were indeed destined for death.
From the serpent Nāga, he obtained a boon and the promise of safety from snakes; remember this.
Trasaddasyu, the son of Pūrukutsa, was the father of Anaraṇya. His son was Haryaśva, from whom came Prāruṇa, and then Tribandhana.
His son was Satyavrata, renowned as Triśaṅku;
having attained the state of a caṇḍāla due to the curse of his guru through the power of Kauśika,
he ascended to heaven in his physical body and is seen in the sky even today.

O Lord, Hariścandra, the son of Triśaṅku, was cast down head-first by the gods and forcibly paralyzed by him; for his sake, there occurred a battle between two birds belonging to Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha that lasted for many years.
Childless and despondent, he sought refuge with Varuṇa at the instruction of Nārada, saying: "O Lord, let a son be born to me;
O Great King, if he is a hero, I shall sacrifice him to you."
Saying "So be it," Varuṇa begat for him a son named Rohita.
Once the son was born, he said, "O dear one, sacrifice me with this [son]. He replied, "When the animal has passed ten days [of birth], then it shall become fit for sacrifice."
When ten days had passed, he arrived and said, "Sacrifice! He replied, "When the teeth of the animal have grown, then it shall become fit for sacrifice.
When the teeth had grown, he replied again, "Sacrifice! Then he spoke.

"When his teeth fall out, then he becomes fit for sacrifice. When the teeth of the animal had fallen out, he said, "Sacrifice! He replied, "When the teeth of the animal grow back again, then the animal is pure."
"Be born again and perform sacrifice," he said; then he replied:
"O King, when a Kṣatriya is fully armored for battle, then his sacrificial animal is pure.
Thus, with a heart constrained by affection through love for his son, he spoke.
While he was thus deceiving Time, the Lord looked upon him;
Rohita, perceiving that and desiring to perform his father’s work,
took up his bow and fled into the forest, seeking to save his life.

Hearing that his father had been seized by Varuṇa and had developed a massive abdominal swelling, Rohita went to a village; Indra, however, forbade him from entering. "Wandering the earth while visiting sacred fords and holy sites is meritorious."
Śakra commanded Rohitā and the others; he too dwelt in the forest for a year.
In this manner, during the second, third, fourth, and likewise the fifth year, the slayer of Vṛtra, having repeatedly approached him, spoke while appearing as an elderly brahmin.
Having spent his sixth year there, Rohita approached the city and purchased from Ajīgarta the middle son,
Śunaḥśepha, as a sacrificial animal; having offered him to his father, he paid his respects.
Then, having been freed from his belly-ache, the highly illustrious Hariścandra, whose stories are great, performed the Puruṣamedha sacrifice for the gods beginning with Varuṇa;
Viśvāmitra was the *hotṛ* priest in that rite, and the self-controlled [Vasiṣṭha] was the *adhvaryu*.
Jamadagni became a Brahmin, as did Vasiṣṭha and Ayāsya, who was a singer of the Sāman hymns;
pleased with him, Indra gave him a chariot made of gold.
The greatness of Śunaḥśepha will be described later.
Seeing the truth, essence, and fortitude of the king together with his wife,
Viśvāmitra was greatly pleased and granted him unimpeded progress:
the mind into the earth, that [earth] into water, the water into fire, and that [fire] into air.
Holding the vital air in the ether, and that [ether] in the *bhūtādi*, and that in the Great Self (*mahātman*);
having meditated upon the digit of knowledge (*jñānakalā*) within that, and completely burning away ignorance with it;
and having abandoned that [ignorance] through his own nature, which is the consciousness of the bliss of liberation (*nirvāṇasukha*).
He remained there, his bonds destroyed, by means of that which is indefinable and beyond the reach of logic.
Śrī Śuka said: Harita was the son of Rohita; from him Campa was produced.
From him came Campāpurī and Sudeva; Vijaya was his son.
Bharuka was his son, from whom came Vṛka, and his son was Bāhuka.
That king, having been deprived of his kingdom by his enemies, entered the forest together with his wife.
When he had grown old and reached the state of death, the queen intended to follow him in death; however, she was dissuaded by Aurva, who knew that she would have offspring.
Having learned of this, her co-wives administered a poison along with some food.
Together with him was born the highly illustrious one named Sagara;
he was the universal emperor (cakravartin) Sagara, after whose sons the ocean was made.
He [conquered] the Tālajaṅghas, Yavanas, Śakas, Haihayas, and Barbaras.
Out of respect for his guru’s word, he did not kill them; instead, he made them wear distorted disguises—
some with shaven heads and beards, some with disheveled hair and half-shaven heads, some without inner garments, and others without outer garments.

He performed horse-sacrifices with the aim of attaining Hari, the Lord and the Self, who is the essence of all Vedas and gods, according to the yoga taught by Aurva. However, Purandara seized the horse intended as the sacrificial victim for that sacrifice.
The sons of Sumati, arrogant yet obedient to their father’s command,
dug up the earth on all sides while searching for the horse.
In the north-eastern direction, near Kapila, they beheld the horse.
"This horse-stealing thief sits here with eyes closed;
let him be killed, let this sinner be killed!"— thus shouting, sixty thousand men with raised weapons rushed toward him, at which time the sage opened his eyes.

While their minds were captivated by Mahendra, those sons of the king of men— who had already been struck down by the transgression against their elder— were reduced to ashes in an instant by the fire of their own bodies. Yet, even as they were consumed by the sage’s wrath, no cry of "this is not right" arose from that abode of goodness.
How can the darkness of anger be perceived in Him whose very self is the purifier of the universe, any more than the dust of the earth can be seen in the sky?

How can there be a sense of separateness in the wise one who has become the Supreme Self— that firm boat consisting of Sāṅkhya philosophy, impelled by whom the seeker of liberation crosses the ocean of worldly existence, that path of death so difficult to traverse?
He who was called Asamañjasa was the son of the king by Keśinī;
his son was named Aṃśumān, who was devoted to the welfare of his grandfather. Asamañjasa revealed himself to be truly inconsistent.
Remembering his previous births, that yogi, having been diverted from yoga by his former attachments,
performed contemptible acts in the world that were disagreeable to his kinsmen; he threw children who were playing in the Sarayū river into the water, causing alarm among the people.
Having behaved in this manner, he was indeed abandoned by his father, who cast aside all affection;
then, having displayed those boys through his yogic power, he departed from there.
All the inhabitants of Ayodhyā [beheld] the boys returned once more.
O King, seeing this, they were struck with wonder, and the king himself was filled with remorse.
Then Aṃśumat, urged by the king, set out in search of the horse;
following the path of his paternal uncle’s trench, he beheld the horse amidst the ashes.
Seeing the sage named Kapila, who was actually the Lord Adhokṣaja, seated there, the great King Aṃśumān,
with a concentrated mind, bowed down with folded hands and offered praise.
Aṃśumān said:

The unevolved soul does not see You, the Supreme Self, nor does it realize You even now through the methods of meditative absorption; how much less so others? We, who are created from the emanations of his mind, body, and intellect, are devoid of light.
Those embodied beings who are dominated by the three modes perceive only the modes themselves, or else they perceive only darkness.

Those whose minds are deluded by Your māyā do not perceive You as established within themselves, for they lack outward illumination; how then can I, being utterly bewildered, contemplate You— who are a mass of pure knowledge, whose nature destroys the delusion of the distinctions among the qualities of māyā, and who are realized by sages such as Sanandana?

We bow to You, the Ancient Person (Puruṣa), whose marks of material nature, qualities, and karma have been stilled; who is beyond name and form, and liberated from both existence and non-existence; and who has assumed a body for the purpose of imparting knowledge.
In this world fashioned by Your Māyā, people perceive houses and other objects as real entities...
They wander with their minds bewildered by lust, greed, envy, and delusion.
O Soul of all beings, today, by the sight of you, O Blessed One, the firm snare of delusion— which consists of desire, action, the senses, and the subconscious mind— has been severed for us.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having thus experienced the power of his song, the blessed sage Kapila, favoring him with his wisdom, spoke these words to Aṃśumat.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O child, let this horse be led away; it is the sacrificial animal for your grandfather.
Moreover, these ancestors have been consumed by fire; they deserve the water of the Gaṅgā and nothing else."

Having circumambulated him and propitiated him by bowing his head, Sagara brought back the horse; with that animal, he completed the remainder of the sacrifice. Having entrusted the kingdom to Aṃśumat, he became free from desire and released from all bonds.
By following the path instructed by Aurva, he attained the supreme goal.
Śrī Śuka said:
And Aṃśumān performed austerities with the desire to bring down the Gaṅgā.
He was unable to endure that great length of time; consequently, he passed away in the course of time.
His son Dilīpa likewise, being unable [to endure it], met his end in due time.
His son Bhagīratha performed most intense austerities.
The Goddess revealed Herself to him, saying, "I am pleased; I am here to grant you a boon.
Thus addressed, the king bowed down and declared his intention:
"Who indeed can sustain my momentum as I fall to the surface of the earth?"
Otherwise, O King, I shall pierce the earth and go to the subterranean realm (rasātala). Furthermore, why should I not go to the earth? For men wipe away their sins upon me;
O King, consider this: where else could I wipe away those sins?
Śrī Bhagīratha said:
The saintly renunciants, peaceful, most devoted to Brahman, and purifiers of the world, remove sin through physical contact; for Hari, the destroyer of sin, dwells within them.

"Rudra, the self of all embodied beings, in whom this entire universe is woven like a cloth upon its threads— he will sustain your force. Having spoken thus, the king gratified the god Śiva through his ascetic penance.
O King, in a very short time the Lord was pleased with him;
"So be it," said Śiva, the benefactor of all the worlds,
and he attentively bore Gaṅgā, whose waters are purified by the feet of Hari.
That royal sage Bhagīratha led the world-purifying Gaṅgā to the place where the bodies of his ancestors lay reduced to ashes;
she followed him as he proceeded by chariot with the speed of the wind.
Purifying the lands, she drenched the sons of Sagara who had been consumed by fire; by the mere touch of her water, even though they had been struck down by the curse of Brahmā,
the sons of Sagara ascended to heaven, leaving behind nothing but the ashes of their bodies.
The sons of Sagara attained heaven merely by contact with his ashes-reduced body;
how much more so for those who, firm in their vows, serve the Goddess with faith?
Indeed, this which has been manifested here by the celestial river is no great wonder.

Fixing their minds with faith upon Him from whose lotus feet the river [Gaṅgā] was born— which severs worldly existence— the stainless sages immediately cast off the three qualities that are so difficult to abandon and attained identity with His very self.

From Śruta was born Bhagīratha; his son was Nābha, and from him came another, Sindhudvīpa. From him was born Ayutāyu, and from him came Ṛtūparṇa, who was a friend of Nala and learned the science of horses from Nala.
Having given him the secret of the dice, he [Vasiṣṭha] granted his son all his desires.
Thereafter, Sudāsa’s son, the king who was the husband of Damayantī,
was known as Ahūrmitra, Sahasra, and also, at times, Kalmāṣapāda.
Due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha and by his own karma, he became a Rakṣasa and remained childless.
King Parīkṣit said:
"O Teacher, for what reason was the curse pronounced upon the high-souled Saudāsa?"
"We wish to know this; let it be told, provided it is not a secret.
Śrī Śuka said:
"Saudāsa, while wandering on a hunt, killed a certain Rākṣasa."
Then, having gone with the desire to retaliate, he released his brother;
while reflecting upon the king’s sin, he, assuming the form of a cook in the palace,
cooked human flesh and brought it to his master who was desirous of eating.
Seeing that which was about to be served, the Blessed One immediately perceived it to be unfit for consumption;
enraged, he cursed the king: "You shall indeed become a *rākṣasa*. Having learned that this had been done by a *rākṣasa*, [the sage] performed a twelve-year sacrifice.
He too, taking water in his cupped hands, prepared to curse his guru;
but restrained by Madayantī, he released the angry waters at his guru's feet,
O King, as he beheld all directions, the sky, the earth, and everything as consisting of living beings.
Having fallen into a demonic state, his foot became spotted with black;
at the time of sexual union, he saw two brahmin forest-dwellers.
Afflicted by hunger, he seized the brahmin, while his wife spoke as if she had accomplished her purpose.
"You are no mere demon; you are a great chariot-warrior among the Ikṣvākus, the heroic husband of Madayantī. O hero, you ought not to commit unrighteousness.
Give back to me, who desire offspring, my husband, that twice-born man whose purpose remains unfulfilled."
"O King, this human body bestows all goals upon a person;
therefore, O hero, the killing of it is said to be the destruction of all goals.
For this man is a learned brāhmaṇa, endowed with the virtues of austerity and good character."
Desiring to worship the Brahman known as the Mahāpuruṣa—
who is hidden within all beings by means of his qualities through the state of being the Self of all beings—
that very best of Brahman-sages [approached] you, O Lord, from among the most eminent of royal sages.

O knower of dharma, how can he deserve death, like a son [desiring] his father? How do you, who are honored by the virtuous, consider the slaughter of that saintly, sinless child who was a teacher of the Veda, just as one might consider the slaughter of Babhru?
"If he is to be eaten, then eat me first;
without him I shall not live for even a moment, like one who is already dead.
Thus she lamented, speaking with compassion like one who is helpless.
Like a tiger devouring its prey, Saudāsa, deluded by a curse,
devoured the Brāhmaṇī Didhiṣū; seeing her thus consumed by the man-eater, she,
filled with rage, cursed the lord of the earth for his own soul.
"O sinful one, since you have devoured my husband while I was afflicted by desire,
death has been shown to you as well, O man of unrefined intellect, through the very act of impregnation.
Having thus cursed Mitrasaha, she, who was solely devoted to the world of her husband, departed.
Having cast her husband's bones into a well-kindled fire, she attained the same destination as her lord.
At the end of twelve years, freed from the curse and intent upon sexual union,
he informed her of the Brahmin’s curse and was restrained by the queen.

From that time forward, he abandoned the pleasure of women and, being childless by his own karma, Vasiṣṭha— having been authorized by him— procreated offspring through Madayantī. She indeed carried the fetus for seven years, yet she did not give birth.
He struck her womb with a stone; because of that, he is called Aśmaka.
From Aśmaka was born Bālika, who was protected by women and thus called Nārīkavaca; when the warrior class had vanished, he became Mūlaka.
From him came Daśaratha, from whom was born the son Aiḍaviḍi;
from him came King Viśvasaha, whose son was the universal emperor Khaṭvāṅga,
who, being difficult to conquer, slew the Daityas in battle when entreated by the gods.
Realizing his life span was but a moment, he returned to his own city and fixed his mind upon it:
"Neither my life-breaths from the family of Brahmā, nor my sons who are the deities of my lineage, nor my fortunes, nor the earth, nor my kingdom, nor even my wife are as dear to me as they were."
Even in my childhood, my mind never took pleasure in unrighteousness anywhere;
nor did I ever perceive any object other than the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka).
A boon was granted to me by the gods, the lords of the three worlds, according to my desire.
I do not choose that desire, for I am the contemplator of the Creator of all beings.
Even the gods, whose senses and intellects are distracted, do not find the Beloved who eternally resides within their own hearts— the Self— how much less so others?

"Having abandoned attachment to the qualities fashioned by the Lord's *māyā*— which are like a city of the Gandharvas— and having renounced that [attachment] rooted in the self of material nature through devotion to the Creator of the universe, I take refuge in Him.
Thus he resolved with a mind grasped by Nārāyaṇa.
Having abandoned other states of being and ignorance, he then established himself in his own true nature—
that which is Brahman, supreme and subtle, non-empty yet conceived as empty,
whom the Sātvatas indeed proclaim as the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
Śrī Śuka said: From Khaṭvāṅga was born Dīrghabāhu, from him Raghu, from him Pṛthuśravas,
from him the great king Aja, and from him Daśaratha was born.
To him also, this Lord Hari, who is composed of Brahman,
appeared in person as a portion of a portion, having been requested by the gods to become their son under the names Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna.

O King, the life-story of that Lord of Sītā has been heard and described at length by the seers who perceive the truth; you have heard it repeatedly. Having renounced his kingdom for the sake of his guru, he wandered through the forest on the lotus-like feet of his beloved.

May the Lord of Kosala protect us—he who, by the touch of his hand, wiped away the pain from the path for the two younger brothers of Indra; he whose knitting of the eyebrows was provoked by the anger of separation from his beloved due to the deformity of Śūrpaṇakhā; he who, terrified the ocean and built the bridge; and he who is the forest fire to the wicked.
By him, at the sacrifice of Viśvāmitra, the foremost of the Nairṛtas— the night-stalking followers of Mārīca—
were slain even as Lakṣmaṇa looked on;
he who, in the assembly of the world’s heroes, [broke] the formidable bow of Śiva.

O King, like a young elephant playfully seizing a stalk of sugarcane, he took up the bow that had been brought by three hundred men in the hall of Sītā’s svayaṃvara, strung it, and broke it in the middle.
Having conquered [Rāvaṇa] and obtained Sītā— whose name signifies Fortune herself, who possessed corresponding beauty, character, youth, and form, and who was the very pride upon his chest—
he proceeded along the path of the Lord of the Bhṛgus and removed the deep-rooted [grief].

He who, though accompanied by his wife, humbled the pride of the earth by three times uprooting the seed of the kings, and who, bound by the noose of truth, accepted the command of his father even when it was influenced by a woman.

Having abandoned his kingdom, royal fortune, beloved friends, and his residence, he went to the forest like one who has renounced all attachments, as if discarding his very life-breaths. He assumed a form [befitting] the sister of the Rākṣasa, for her intellect was impure.
With bow in hand, he slew her fourteen thousand kinsmen, headed by Khara, Triśiras,
and Dūṣaṇa; though invincible, he dwelt there in distress while crying out.
O King, having seen that [deer] created by the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, whose heart-fire was inflamed by hearing the story of Sītā,
he was drawn away from his hermitage and slain by that being in the form of a wondrous deer.
Just as the fierce Indra swiftly struck Mārīca with his arrow, so too,
while the daughter of the King of Videha was being led away by that lowest of Rākṣasas like a wolf in the forest, he acted in her absence.

Separated from his beloved wife in the forest like a wretched man by his brother, he wandered about, demonstrating the fate of those attached to women; meanwhile, having burned Kabandha, who had ruined his own purpose with his own actions, he performed a great deed.

Having established friendship with those monkeys and learned from them the whereabouts of his beloved, and after Vālin had been slain by the monkey-lord’s army, that Manu, whose feet are worshipped by the lotus-born Brahmā, reached the shore.

The ocean, personified, bearing upon his head the offering of worship, was filled with the cries of terror as its crocodiles and sea-monsters were thrown into confusion by the falling of her sidelong glances, which were rolling with the agitation of her wrath.
Approaching his lotus feet, he spoke thus:
"O Infinite One, we of dull intellect did not truly know you—
the immutable, the primordial Person, the sovereign Lord of all worlds."
From whose *sattva* the hosts of gods arise, from whose *rajas* the lords of creatures, and from whose *manas* the lords of beings— He, the Lord of the Guṇas, is Your Honor.
Go at will and destroy this contemptuous act of Viśravas.
"O hero, obtain Rāvaṇa, the terror of the three worlds, as your wife;
build a bridge here for the expansion of your fame,
which kings who have conquered the quarters sing of upon approaching."
The Lord of the Raghus, having constructed a bridge across the great ocean with the peaks of various mountains—
the trunks of which were shaken by the hands of the monkey leaders—
accompanied by his armies headed by Sugrīva, Nīla, and Hanumān.

He entered Laṅkā, which had been scorched by the sight of Vibhīṣaṇa; its pleasure gardens and storehouses were blocked by the army of the lord of monkeys, and its glorious gates, towers, halls, balconies, and pinnacles were destroyed.
With its chariot-poles, banners, and golden jars being shattered,
the city was like a river agitated by herds of elephants; seeing this, Nikumbha and Kumbha, the lords of the Rākṣasas, [acted].
Then he dispatched Dhūmrākṣa, Durmukha, Surāntaka, Narāntaka, and others;
his son Prahasta, Atikāya, Vikampana, and others;
and all his followers, as well as Kumbhakarṇa.
That army of Yātudhānas was difficult to traverse due to its swords, spears, bows, javelins, *prāsa* darts,
*śakti* missiles, arrows, *tomara* lances, and swords;
yet Sugrīva, Lakṣmaṇa, Hanumān the son of the Maruts, and Gandhamādana—
Accompanied by Nīla, Aṅgada, Ṛkṣa, Panasa, and others, he advanced;
all those commanders of the divisions of the Lord of the Raghus, having charged forward,
engaged in pairwise combat with their respective units of elephant-riders, infantry, charioteers, and horsemen.
Aṅgada and the others struck with trees, mountain peaks, clubs,
and arrows the lords of Rāvaṇa, whose auspiciousness had been destroyed by their assault on Sītā.
Seeing the destruction of his own army, the lord of the Rākṣasas became enraged.
Then, having mounted his chariot, he rushed toward Rāma;
in that radiant celestial vehicle brought by Mātali,
he struck the brilliantly shining one with sharp, razor-edged arrows.
Rāma said to him: "O manure of a human being!
This is the fruit today for you, who are devoid of shame and loathsome, that our beloved was snatched away like a dog by a wicked person in our very presence."
"Like Time itself, whose power is insurmountable for the doer, I shall strike him down. Thus speaking, he released from his bow the arrow he had fixed,
which, like a thunderbolt, pierced his heart.
Vomiting blood, he fell from his celestial chariot while the people cried out "Alas! like a virtuous man who has been stripped of his merit;
then, thousands of Rākṣasa women emerged from Laṅkā.
Together with Mandodarī, they rushed there weeping aloud; embracing their respective kinsmen who were afflicted by Lakṣmaṇa’s arrows, they, being wretched,
wept piteously while striking themselves with their own hands.
"Alas! We are undone, O Lord, O Rāvaṇa who causes the world to cry out! To whom shall Laṅkā go for refuge when it is abandoned by you and oppressed by enemies?
O highly fortunate one, having fallen under the sway of passion, you truly do not understand."
O delighter of your lineage, by the power of Sītā’s splendor you have been brought to this state; Lankā has been made a widow,
and we ourselves have been turned into food for vultures, while your body has become a cause for your own descent into hell.
Śrī Śuka said:
With the approval of the Lord of Kosala, Vibhīṣaṇa performed for his kinsmen the funeral rites according to the injunctions for the afterlife as prescribed in the Pitṛmedha.
Then, in the hermitage of the Aśoka grove, the Blessed One saw her—
emaciated by the disease of separation from him— reclining at the foot of a śiṃśapā tree; and seeing his most beloved wife so distressed, Rāma was deeply moved with compassion.
Having seated his two brothers, whose lotus-faces were blooming with the joy of beholding him, upon the vehicle that shone like Hanumān,
the Blessed Lord ascended it; he had already bestowed upon Vibhīṣaṇa the lordship over the hosts of Rākṣasas.
Having completed his vow, he went to the city of Laṅkā, which lasted until the end of the kalpa;
on the way, he was showered with beautiful flowers offered by the guardians of the worlds,
while his deeds were joyfully sung by Śatadhṛti and the other gods.

Having heard that his brother was wearing bark garments, subsisting on barley-gruel mixed with cow-urine, matted-haired, and sleeping on the bare ground, the deeply compassionate Bharata— upon learning of his arrival— was filled with distress along with the citizens, ministers, and family priests.

Placing the sandals upon his head, he went out from his own camp at Nandigrāma to meet his elder brother Rāma, amidst the sounds of singing and musical instruments and the frequent chanting of the Vedas by those who discourse on Brahman.
With chariots adorned with golden girths and banners, featuring variegated flags made of gold; with excellent horses, warriors clad in golden armor and wearing golden breastplates;
and with processions of eminent courtesans and attendant followers.
Taking up the insignia of the supreme lordship and various other commodities,
his heart and eyes overflowing with love, he fell at his feet;
placing the sandals before him, he stood with palms joined in reverence and eyes filled with tears.
Embracing him for a long time with both arms and bathing him with tears from his eyes,
Rāma— himself already saluted by the subjects— paid homage to those brāhmaṇas who were the most worthy among the worthy, along with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā.
Shaking their upper garments and scattering flowers as they beheld their lord returned after a long time, the people of Northern Kosala danced with joy;
Bharata took up his sandals and held the two excellent yak-tail fans.

O King, Vibhīṣaṇa held the white parasol along with Sugrīva; the son of the Maruts (Hanumān) bore the bow and quivers; Śatrughna carried Sītā as his sacred water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); Aṅgada bore a golden sword, and the leaders of the bears carried shields.
Seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot, praised by women and extolled by bards,
the Blessed One shone, O King, like the risen moon among the planets.
Then, welcomed by his brother, he entered the city amidst great festivities.

Having entered the royal palace, he— being honored in turn— paid homage to the wives of his elders, his own mother, his teachers, and his peers and juniors; Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa likewise approached them in the prescribed manner.
Their mothers, rising up as if their very lives had returned to them, placed their sons upon their laps and,
bathing them with floods of tears, cast off their grief.
Then the Guru, having formally untied his matted locks along with the elders of the lineage, performed the rites according to tradition.
He consecrated him just as Indra was consecrated with the waters of the four oceans and other substances.
Having thus performed his ceremonial bath on the head, well-dressed, garlanded, and adorned,
he shone together with his brothers and his wife, who were likewise well-adorned and finely attired.

Having been propitiated by his brother with prostrations, Rāma accepted the throne. He protected the subjects—who were devoted to their own duties and endowed with the virtues appropriate to their social class and stage of life—just like a father; and they regarded him as their father.
While Tretā-yuga was prevailing, time became equal to that of Kṛta-yuga,
because King Rāma was a knower of dharma who brought happiness to all living beings.
Forests, rivers, mountains, regions, islands, and oceans [all flourished].
O bull of the Bharata lineage, all cows were wish-fulfilling for the subjects;
there was no mental anguish, physical disease, old age, exhaustion, suffering, grief, fear, or fatigue,
nor was there death for those who did not desire it, while Adhokṣaja was king in Rāma.
Observing the vow of having only one wife, pure and following the conduct of royal sages, he himself practiced the duties of a householder to teach them by example. The virtuous Satī,
bowed down with love, devotion, good character, and humility, [attended him].
Out of fear and shame, Sītā, perceiving the state of her husband’s mind as he was about to abduct her, [remained silent].
Śrī Śuka said:
The Blessed Lord Rāma, by means of his own self, [manifested himself] with supreme celestial ornaments.
Then, under the guidance of his preceptor, he worshipped with sacrifices that God who embodies all the gods.
The Lord gave the eastern direction as a sacrificial fee to the *hotṛ*, the southern to the *brahman*,
the western to the *adhvaryu*, and the northern to the singer of the *sāmans*.

He gave the remainder of the earth, however much remained within its bounds, to his teacher, thinking: "A Brahmin who is free from desire deserves all this. Thus, he was left with nothing but his ornaments and two garments.
Likewise, Queen Vaidehī alone remained, protected by her auspicious marriage-thread.
Having observed the praised affection of the divine Brāhmaṇa,
they were pleased and, with hearts melting with emotion, returned [the child] to him and spoke as follows:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the World, what indeed have you not bestowed upon us,
since you enter our inner hearts and destroy our darkness with your own radiance? Homage to Rāma, the deity devoted to Brahman, whose intellect is unimpeded."

Once, desiring to know the world, Rāma wandered about in secret, unobserved during the night; he overheard the words of a certain man addressed to his wife concerning the preeminent Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka), to whom all violence has been surrendered and upon whose feet all have placed their burden.
"I do not maintain you, for you are wicked, unchaste, and have gone to the house of another.
For it is only one who is dominated by women who would maintain Sītā; I shall not accept her again.
Thus [he spoke] from the world at large, which was hostile in many ways, difficult to propitiate, and ignorant.

Abandoned by her husband out of fear, she reached the hermitage of Prācetasa; when the time had come, being pregnant, she gave birth to twin sons. Renowned as Kuśa and Lava, the sage performed their sacramental rites for them.
Aṅgada and Citraketu are recorded as the two sons of Lakṣmaṇa; O lord of the earth, Takṣa and Puṣkala were the two sons of Bharata;
and Subāhu and Śrutasena were the two sons of Śatrughna.
Bharata slew crores of Gandharvas during his conquest of the directions;
having brought all their wealth, he presented it to the King.
And Śatrughna [slew] the Rākṣasa named Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu.
Having slain [the demons] in Madhuvana, he established the city named Mathurā. Sītā, having been exiled by her husband while the sage was away,
entered a cave while meditating upon the feet of Rāma.
Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Rāma, though restraining his grief with his intellect,
was unable to suppress those various memories of her qualities, even though he was the Supreme Controller. Such an intimacy between a woman and a man brings terror everywhere.
This is true even for the lords of the gods, let alone for an ordinary person whose mind is fixed on the household life.
Thereafter, maintaining his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*),
the Lord performed the *agnihotra* sacrifice uninterruptedly for thirteen thousand years.
Placing his own sprout-like foot, which had been pierced by the thorns of the Daṇḍaka forest, upon the hearts of those who remember Him, Rāma, the light of the Self, then departed from there.
This is not the only glory of the Lord of the Raghus; He did not take up [the earth] merely at the request of the gods.
For Him whose abode is free from even the slightest inequality due to His playful body,
what need was there for weapons to slay the demon, or for monkeys as allies in the destruction of His enemies during the binding of the ocean?

Whose stainless fame, which destroys all sins, even now the sages sing in the assemblies of kings as the head-ornament of the lordly elephants of the quarters; he who is honored by the crowns of the guardians of heaven and the lords of wealth— [to him I bow].
I take refuge in the lotus feet of the Lord of the Raghus;
those Kosalas whom He touched, or by whom He was seen, or who sat with Him, or even followed Him, have gone to that abode where the yogis go.
O King, a person who, being devoted to compassion, listens with their ears and internalizes the deeds of Rāma, is liberated from the bonds of karma. Śrī Rājā said:

"How did the Blessed Lord Rāma behave toward his brothers, or how did he behave toward himself? And how did they, as well as the subjects and the citizens, conduct themselves toward that Lord? Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Then the Lord of the three worlds commanded his brothers to go forth on the conquest of the quarters; meanwhile, revealing himself to his own people, he beheld his city with his attendants.
Its streets were sprinkled with scented water and the ichor-drops from the temples of elephants.
Seeing her husband arrived, she was as if even more intoxicated; meanwhile,
the palaces, gateways, assembly halls, shrines, temples, and other structures were adorned with golden jars placed upon them and decorated with banners.
With clusters of plantains still on their stalks, with strips of fine cloth,
mirrors, silken garments, and garlands, they constructed festive archways; there, the citizens approached him from place to place, bearing offerings in their hands.
"O Lord, grant us our blessings; protect this earth which was previously uplifted by you.

Then, seeing their lord returned after a long time, the women and men—having abandoned their homes out of a desire to see him—ascended their palaces and, with eyes that could not look enough, showered the lotus-eyed one with flowers.
Then he entered his own palace, which had been inhabited by his predecessors, and was enriched with inexhaustible treasuries and costly, magnificent furnishings;
it featured doors made of coral and udumbara wood and rows of pillars of vaidūrya stone.
