With floors of clear emeralds and walls of shining crystal,
adorned with variegated garlands, friezes, and cloths of many gems and jewels, it was filled with pearls and the radiant splendors that fulfill all desires.
Adorned with fragrant incense and lamps, and decorated with floral ornaments,
the place was graced by men and women who resembled gods and were themselves adorned with jewels.
There, the Blessed Lord Rāma, together with his beloved and cherished wife, [entered].

The bull among those who find delight in their own Self sported with Sītā, and he enjoyed his desires at the proper times without violating dharma for many series of years— he whose sprout-like feet were longed for by men.
Śrī Śuka said: From Kuśa came Atithi; from him Niṣadha; his son was Nabha;
then Puṇḍarīka was his son, and from him Kṣemadhanvā arose.
From him came Devānīka; from him, Anīha; then his son was Pāriyātra.
From him came Balasthala, and from him Vajranābha, who was born of the Sun (Arka). Sagaṇa was his son, and from him Vidhṛti became the son.

From him was born Hiraṇyanābha, who was a teacher of yoga and the disciple of Jaimini; from him, Yājñavalkya of Kauśala learned the supreme yoga that severs the knots of the heart concerning the supreme self.
Puṣpa was the son of Hiraṇyanābha; from him Dhruvasandhi was born.
Then came Sudarśana, then Agnivarṇa, and his son was Śīghra, whose son was Maru.
That very Maru, having attained perfection in yoga, resides established in the village of Kalāpa.
At the end of the Kali age, he will restore the solar dynasty which had perished.
From him [will come] Prasuśruta; his son will be Sandhi, and his son will be Amarṣaṇa.
Mahasvān will be his son, and from him Viśvabāhu was born.
From him, Prasena-jit will arise, and from him Takṣaka will be born again.
Then there will be Bṛhad-bala, who was slain by your father in battle. These are the Ikṣvāku kings who have passed away; now hear of those yet to come.
The son of Bṛhadbala will be named Bṛhadraṇa; his son will be Ūrukriya, and his son will be Vatsavṛddha. From him will come Prativyoma, then Bhānu, Divāka, and Vāhinīpati.
From him shall come the hero Sahadeva, then Bṛhadaśva, then Bhānumat;
from Bhānumat shall come Pratīkāśva, and his son shall be Supratīka. Then there will be Marudeva, then Sunakṣatra, and then Puṣkara.
His son was Antarikṣa; his son was Sutapas, who conquered his enemies.
Bṛhadrāja was his son, and from him came Barhiṣmat; from him Kṛtañjaya was born. Raṇañjaya was his son, and from him Sañjaya will arise.
From him [Śākya] shall come Śuddhodana; his son is recorded as Lāṅgala. From him will arise Prasenajit, and from him Kṣudraka.
From him Raṇaka will arise, and Suratha will be his son.

Sumitra by name will be the last; these are the descendants of Bṛhadbala. This lineage of the Ikṣvākus shall end with Sumitra, for upon reaching that king, it will indeed come to an end in the Kali age.
Śrī Śuka said:
Nimi, the son of Ikṣvāku, chose Vasiṣṭha as his officiating priest (ṛtvij).
Having begun the sacrificial session (satra), he [Vasiṣṭha] replied: "O sir, I have already been chosen by Indra."
"Having completed that [sacrifice], I shall return; meanwhile, wait for me.
The householder remained silent;
he too, being self-possessed and knowing this world to be transient, commenced a sacrificial session (*satra*).
Meanwhile, while the other officiating priests were still occupied,
the Guru, having observed the transgression of his disciple, returned; seeing Nimi, who considered himself a scholar, he cursed him, saying, "May the body of this one fall down!"
Nimi cast back the curse upon his preceptor, who had acted unrighteously:
"May your body also fall, for you do not know dharma and have acted out of greed.
Having said this, Nimi, who was proficient in the science of the self, cast off his own body.
The great-grandfather was born from Urvaśī by Mitra and Varuṇa;
O best of sages, having deposited his body among the fragrant substances when the sacrificial session was concluded,
he spoke to the assembled gods.
"If my lords are pleased, let this body of the king live.
When they replied, "So be it," Nimi said: "May I have no further bondage to a body—[a body] from which those who are terrified by the fear of separation do not desire union."
The sages of purified intellect worship the lotus feet of Hari;
I do not desire this body which brings about misery, grief, and fear,
since death is everywhere for it, just as it is for fish in the water.
The gods said:
"O Videha, may you dwell at will within the eyes of embodied beings; established in the inner self, you shall be perceived by the opening and closing of their eyelids."
Perceiving the fear of anarchy among men, the great seers churned the body of Nimi; from it a prince was born.
By virtue of his birth he became Janaka, while Vaideha was so called because he was born from Videha.
Mithila was born from Mathana; he by whom Mithilā was built.
From him came Udāvasu, whose son was Nandivardhana. After him came Suketu, and his son, O King, was Devarāta.
From him [Bṛhatkṣatra] was born Bṛhadratha; his father was Mahāvīrya Sudhṛt.
From Sudhṛt was born Dhṛṣṭaketu, then Haryaśva, and from him Maru. From Maru was born Pratīpaka, and from him was born Kṛtaratha.
Deva-mīḍha was his son, and then there was the renowned Mahādhṛti.
From him came Kṛtirāta, and his son was Mahāromā.
Svarṇaromā was his son, and from him Hrasvaromā was born.
From him was born Śīradhvaja, who ploughed the earth for the sake of sacrifice;
Sītā was born from the tip of his ploughshare, and therefore he is known as Śīradhvaja.
His son was Kuśadhvaja, and from him came King Dharmadhvaja.
Dharmadhvaja had two sons, Kṛtadhvaja and Mitadhvaja. From Kṛtadhvaja was born Keśidhvaja, and from Mitadhvaja came Khāṇḍikya; O King, the son of Kṛtadhvaja was a master of self-knowledge.
Khāṇḍikya, who was an expert in the true nature of ritual action, fled in fear from Keśidhvaja.
His son was Bhānumant, and his son was Śatadyumna. From him came Śuci, and from him Sanadvāja was born as a son.
From Sanadvāja was born Ūrjaketu; his son was Aja, and his son was Purujit.
From him came Ariṣṭanemi, whose son was Śrutāyu, and his son was Supārśvaka.
From him came Citraratha, whose son was Kṣemādi, the lord of Mithilā.
From him came Samaratha; his son was Satyaratha.
From him came Upagu, and from him Upagupta, who was born of Agni.
Then Vasvānanta was his son, and his son was Yuyudha, who was eloquent in speech.
From him was born Śruta; from him, Vijaya; and from him, the son Ṛta. Śunaka was born as his son, and from him came Vītahavya and Dhṛti.
Bahulāśva was the son of Dhṛti, and Kṛti was his son, who possessed great self-control.
"O King, these people of Mithilā were indeed experts in the knowledge of the Self;
by the grace of the Lord of Yoga, they were liberated from dualities even while living in their homes.
Śrī Śuka said:
Now, therefore, O King, hear the purifying lineage of Soma,
in which kings such as Aila and others of meritorious fame are celebrated.
[It originated] from the lotus in the lake of the navel of the thousand-headed Puruṣa.
To the Creator (Dhātṛ) was born a son, Atri, who was equal to his father in virtues.
From his eyes, it is said, was born a son, Soma, composed of nectar,
whom Brahmā appointed as the lord of the twice-born, of medicinal herbs, and of the hosts of stars.
Having conquered the three worlds, he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice;
out of pride, he forcibly seized Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati.
When he was repeatedly entreated by the preceptor of the gods, he did not desist because of his arrogance.
For his sake, he did not abandon [the sacrifice], and thus the conflict between the gods and the Dānavas arose;
out of hatred for Bṛhaspati, Śukra seized the moon belonging to the Asuras,
while Hara, surrounded by hosts of all beings, took the preceptor’s son out of affection.
Accompanied by all the hosts of gods, Mahendra followed his preceptor. A battle ensued, known as the Tārakāmaya, which brought about the destruction of both gods and demons.
Then, having rebuked Soma, the Creator of All (Brahmā) was informed of the situation by Aṅgiras.
Tārā gave [the child] to her own husband; the husband, realizing she was pregnant, said:
"Abandon, abandon him quickly, O woman of evil intellect! He has been sown in my field by others. I will not reduce you to ashes, for there is no offspring of your own."
Ashamed, Tārā abandoned the boy who possessed the luster of gold;
both Aṅgiras and Soma felt a longing for the child.
As they disputed loudly over him, saying, "He is mine, not yours," [the boy rose up].
The sages and the gods questioned her, but she, being ashamed, said nothing at all.
Then the boy, provoked by her false modesty, said to his mother: "O woman of wicked conduct, why do you not speak? Tell me quickly of your own fault!"
Brahmā summoned her to a private place and questioned her, consoling her; she spoke softly, saying, "It was Soma's," and Soma then accepted her.
O King, the Self-born One gave her the name Budha.
By that son of profound intellect, who brought joy even to the gods,
Purūravas was born from Ilā, as has been described;
[the father beheld] his beauty, virtues, magnanimity, character, wealth, and prowess.

Having heard Urvaśī being sung of by the celestial sage in the abode of Indra, the goddess, afflicted by the arrows of Love, approached his presence; she had descended to the world of men due to the curse of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Having beheld that best of men, who was like Kandarpa incarnate,
the woman steadied her resolve and approached his presence.
Beholding her, the king’s eyes blossomed with joy.
With his hair standing on end from joy, he spoke to the goddess in gentle words.
Śrī Rājā said:
"Welcome to you, O lady of beautiful hips; please be seated. What may we do for you?"
"Delight yourself with me; let our union last for eternal years.
Urvaśī said:
"O handsome one, whose mind and gaze would not be captivated by you?"
"O dear one, when a man moves from one limb to another out of a desire for pleasure, he falls [from his vow].
O King, giver of honor, please protect these two lambs as a trust;
I shall enjoy myself with you, for you are considered the most praiseworthy of men among women."

"O hero, let ghee be my food, and I shall not look upon you except during sexual union. "So be it," the high-minded one agreed. "Oh, what beauty! Oh, what disposition—truly enchanting to the world of men!"
What man would not serve you, O Goddess, who have come to him of your own accord?
That best of men enjoyed himself as was fitting with her, who delights him,
in the celestial pleasure gardens such as Caitraratha and others, according to his desire.
Delighting with that goddess, whose fragrance was like the filaments of a lotus, and captivated by the scent of her breath, he rejoiced for many days.
Not seeing Urvaśī, Indra urged the Gandharvas on.
"Without Urvaśī, this assembly hall does not shine for me.
Then, when the great night had arrived and darkness was present, they approached and stole the two rams that had been placed there by the king’s wife for Urvaśī.
Hearing the wailing of her two sons as they were being led away, the queen cried out:
"I am destroyed by this wretched protector, a eunuch who fancies himself a hero!
Because of my trust in him, I have been ruined and my children have been stolen by bandits."
Struck by the arrows of her words— “He who lies at night terrified like a woman, and by day like a man”— he was like an elephant pierced by sharp shafts;
taking up his sword at night, he ran toward her in his nakedness, filled with rage.
Having released them there upon the ground, they flashed like lightning;
taking up the two rams, she beheld her husband approaching naked.
Aila, too, not seeing his wife on the bed, became as if despondent.

With his mind fixed on her, distraught and grieving, he wandered the earth like a madman. Seeing her at Kurukṣetra and her five companions by the Sarasvatī river, Purūravas, with a joyful countenance, spoke these well-composed verses: "O you who are as beautiful as the moon, where have you gone? O you whose face is like the full moon, why do you not look upon me? O you whose eyes are like lotus petals, O you who are as lovely as the moon, where are you? O you who are as fair as the moon, where have you gone? O you who are as radiant as the moon, where are you? O you who are as charming as the moon, where are you? O you who are as delightful as the moon, where are you? O you who are as sweet as the moon, where are you? O you who are as enchanting as the moon, where are you? O you who are as captivating as the moon, where are you? O you who are as alluring as the moon, where are you? O you who are as bewitching as the moon, where are you? O you who are as entrancing as the moon, where are you? O you who are as seductive as the moon, where are you? O you who are as ravishing as the moon, where are you? O you who are as intoxicating as the moon, where are you? O you who are as exhilarating as the moon, where are you? O you who are as ecstatic as the moon, where are you? O you who are as blissful as the moon, where are you? O you who are as joyous as the moon, where are you? O you who are as delightful as the moon, where are you? O you who are as pleasant as the moon, where are you? O you who are as agreeable as the moon, where are you? O you who are as pleasing as the moon, where are you? O you who are as dear as the moon, where are you? O you who are as beloved as the moon, where are you? O you who are as cherished as the moon, where are you? O you who are as favored as the moon, where are you? O you who are as adored as the moon, where are you? O you who are as esteemed as the moon, where are you? O you who are as honored as the moon, where are you? O you who are as revered as the moon, where are you? O you who are as worshiped as the moon, where are you? O you who are as venerated as the moon, where are you? O you who are as exalted as the moon, where are you? O you who are as sublime as the moon, where are you? O you who are as supreme as the moon, where are you? O you who are as unsurpassed as the moon, where are you? O you who are as peerless as the moon, where are you? O you who are as incomparable as the moon, where are you? O you who are as matchless as the moon, where are you? O you who are as unique as the moon, where are you? O you who are as singular as the moon, where are you? O you who are as one-in-a-million as the moon, where are you? O you who are as rare as the moon, where are you? O you who are as extraordinary as the moon, where are you? O you who are as marvelous as the moon, where are you? O you who are as wondrous as the moon, where are you? O you who are as miraculous as the moon, where are you? O you who are as prodigious as the moon, where are you? O you who are as astonishing as the moon, where are you? O you who are as incredible as the moon, where are you? O you who are as unbelievable as the moon, where are you? O you who are as unfathomable as the moon, where are you? O you who are as mysterious as the moon, where are you? O you who are as enigmatic as the moon, where are you? O you who are as inscrutable as the moon, where are you? O you who are as inscrutable as the moon, where are you? O you who are as unfathomable as the moon, where are you? O you who are as profound as the moon, where are you? O you who are as deep as the moon, where are you? O you who are as bottomless as the moon, where are you? O you who are as limitless as the moon, where are you? O you who are as boundless as the moon, where are you? O you who are as infinite as the moon, where are you? O you who
"Oho! My wife! Stay, stay, O cruel one! You ought not to abandon me;
even now, before you have reached your goal, let us exchange words.
This beautiful body here falls down, O Goddess, having been carried far away by you."
"Wolves and vultures devour him; he is not a fit recipient for your grace.
Urvaśī said:
"Do not die! You are a man; let these wolves not eat you."
There is no friendship at all among women, for their hearts are like those of wolves.
Indeed, women are merciless, cruel, intolerant, and prone to rash acts;
they will kill even a trusting husband or brother for the sake of a trifle.
Having created false confidence in the ignorant, those unchaste women of independent conduct have abandoned their friendship; desiring ever-new [lovers],
O Lord, at the end of the year you will indeed stay with me for a single night.
"O sir, he will take his pleasure with you, and you shall have other offspring as well. Perceiving that the queen was pregnant, he departed for his city;
and having returned there at the end of a year, he approached Urvaśī, the mother of heroes.
Having found her, he dwelt with her that night filled with joy;
then Urvaśī spoke to him, who was miserable and distressed by separation:
"Follow these Gandharvas; they will give me back to you."
O King, while he was thus offering praise, they were pleased and gave him a vessel of fire.
Thinking it to be Urvaśī, he wandered in the forest and realized his mistake.
Leaving the vessel in the forest, he went home and meditated upon her throughout the night.
When the Tretā age had begun, the triple Veda appeared within his mind.
Having observed that the Aśvattha tree was situated within the womb of the Śamī tree,
he fashioned two fire-drills from it, desiring the world of Urvaśī.

Meditating upon Urvaśī with mantras, the Lord took the lower and upper kindling woods; between the two, he placed himself as the source of procreation. From the friction of these, Jātavedas, the radiant fire, was born.
By means of the triple Vedic knowledge, he was appointed by the king as his son; as Trivṛt,
he performed sacrifices for the Lord Adhokṣaja, the master of sacrifice,
who embodies all the gods, seeking the world of Urvaśī.
In the beginning, O King, there was only one Veda, the *praṇava*, which comprises all speech;

there was only one god, Nārāyaṇa, and no other; and there was only one fire and one social class (*varṇa*). At the onset of the Tretā-yuga, however, the threefold Veda (*trayī*) belonged solely to Purūravas.
Through Agni and his progeny, the king attained the world of the Gandharvas.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
O King, six sons were born to Aila from the womb of Urvaśī.
Āyu, Śrutāyu, Satyāyu, Raya, Vijaya, and Jaya were his sons. Vasumān was the son of Śrutāyu, and Śrutañjaya was the son of Satyāyu.
There was one son of Raya, and the son of Jaya was Amita.
Bhīma was the son of Vijaya, and from him came Kāñcana, who was the *hotraka*.
His son was Jahnu, who drank the Gaṅgā after taking it into his mouthful. From Jahnu came Puru, and his sons were Balāka and Ajaka.
From him came Kuśa; Kuśa’s son was Kuśāmbu, and his sons were Vasu and Kuśanābha—these four. Gādhi was born from Kuśāmbu.
To him, the twice-born Ṛcīka requested his daughter Satyavatī as a bride.
Considering the boon to be unsuitable, Gādhi spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"O Kuśikas, let a thousand horses, moon-bright and each with one black ear, be given as the bride-price for the maiden; we are the lineage of Kuśika."
Having been addressed thus, and having understood his intention, he went into the presence of Varuṇa;
bringing those horses and giving them [to him], he married the lovely-faced woman.
That sage, being entreated by his wife and his mother-in-law out of a desire for offspring, [consented].
Having cooked the *caru* with both sets of mantras, the sage went to bathe. Meanwhile, Satyavatī was asked for her own *caru* by her mother;
considering it to be superior, she offered it to her mother and gave her own portion to her mother instead.
Having learned of that, the sage said to his wife: "You have committed a grievous act;
your son is a formidable wielder of punishment, while your brother is the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman.
Then Bhārgava was pacified by Satyavatī, who said, "Let it not be so."
Then, indeed, Jamadagni became the grandson;
she became the highly meritorious Kauśikī, the purifier of the world.
Jamadagni married Reṇukā, the daughter of Reṇu.
In her were born the sons of the sage Bhārgava, headed by Vasumān;
the youngest among them was born as Rāma, who became renowned by that name.
They say he was a portion of Vāsudeva, the one who brought about the end of the Haihaya dynasty.
He who twenty-one times made this earth devoid of Kṣatriyas destroyed the arrogant warrior class— a burden to the world and hostile to the Brahmanas—
even when their offense was as slight as a mere speck of dust, for they were shrouded in passion and ignorance.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, what was that sin committed by the Kṣatriyas who had not conquered their own selves,
because of which the lineage of the Kṣatriyas was repeatedly destroyed?"
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Arjuna, the lord of the Haihayas and a bull among Kṣatriyas,
having propitiated Datta— an expansion of a portion of Nārāyaṇa— through various services, [attained his goal].
He obtained a thousand arms and invincibility against his enemies,
as well as unimpeded sensory power, vitality, prosperity, splendor, heroism, fame, and strength;
he attained mastery over yoga, sovereignty, and the qualities beginning with *aṇimā*.
Moving with unimpeded gait through the worlds like the wind,
surrounded by jewels of women and intoxicated with passion, he sported in the waters of the Revā;
wearing the Vaijayantī garland, he blocked the river with his arms.
Daśānana, who considered himself a hero, could not endure that prowess of his as his own camp was swept away by the waters of the river flowing against the current;
for he had been captured with ease in the presence of women after having committed an offense.
He by whom [the king] was released when imprisoned at Māhiṣmatī, like a monkey,
once while wandering on a hunt in a lonely forest,
entered by chance the hermitage of Jamadagni.
To that lord of men,
accompanied by his army, ministers, and mounts, the sage whose wealth was asceticism offered the sacrificial oblation.
Indeed, seeing that jewel which surpassed even his own sovereign power, he [was struck with wonder].
Disregarding that, the horse-sacrificer, filled with desire for her,
incited men out of pride to seize the sage’s sacrificial cow;
and they forcibly led her away to Māhiṣmatī along with her calf as she cried out.
Then, after the king had departed, Balarāma arrived at the hermitage;
hearing of that man's wickedness, he became enraged like a struck serpent.
Taking up his terrible axe, along with his quiver, armor, and bow, he set forth.
Like a lion pursuing a leader of the herd, the intolerant king gave chase.
As he was entering the city, the best of the Bhrigus was seen by him— bearing a bow and armed with arrows and axes,
clad in the skin of a black antelope, and adorned with matted locks as radiant as the sun.

He urged forth seventeen most terrifying *akṣauhiṇī* divisions, consisting of elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry, equipped with maces, swords, arrows, spears, *ṛṣṭis*, *śataghnīs*, and *śaktis*; yet the one Blessed Lord Rāma alone destroyed them.
Wherever that destroyer of enemy armies—whose mind and prowess were like the wind—struck with his battle-axe, [the enemy forces perished].
Then, with their arms, thighs, and necks severed, they fell upon the earth, their charioteers and mounts slain;
seeing their own army on the battlefield— mired in the mud of flowing blood— with its armor, banners, bows, and bodies hacked by Rāma’s axes and arrows, the Haihaya king rushed forward in a rage.
Then Arjuna simultaneously fixed arrows upon five hundred bows with his arms; Rāma, the foremost of all wielders of weapons, cut them down at once with a single bow and arrow.
Again, in the battle, he [Arjuna] violently uprooted immovable trees with his own hands and rushed forward in the fray.
With his axe, whose edge was sharp as a thunderbolt, Balarāma violently lopped off the arms of the demon as one might sever the limbs of a serpent.
When his arms were severed, he struck off the demon's head, just as one might cleave a mountain peak.
When their father was slain, his ten thousand sons fled in terror.
Having returned the sacrificial cow along with its calf, the slayer of enemy heroes approached his father’s hermitage and presented the emaciated animal to him;
Rāma then reported that deed of his own to his father and his brothers.
Having heard that, Jamadagni spoke:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, you have committed a sin,
in that you have pointlessly slain a king who embodies all the gods."
"O dear one, we are indeed brāhmaṇas who have attained the state of being worthy of honor through our forbearance (kṣamā)—
by which the Lord, the teacher of the world, attained the station of Brahmā. Through forbearance, the splendor of a brāhmaṇa shines like the radiance of the sun."
Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, is quickly pleased with those who are forgiving. The killing of a consecrated king is a heavier sin than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, my dear one, with your mind fixed on Acyuta, abandon this evil through service to sacred pilgrimage sites.
Śrī Śuka said: O descendant of Kuru, having been thus instructed by his father, Rāma replied, "So be it," and after wandering on a pilgrimage for one year, he returned to the hermitage.
Once, while Reṇukā had gone to the Gaṅgā, she saw the king of the Gandharvas, adorned with a garland of lotuses, sporting with Apsarases. While watching him play, she went to the river for water.
Due to her longing for Citraratha, she did not remember the time for the fire-oblation;
seeing that the time had passed, she became apprehensive of the sage’s curse and,
returning, stood before him with joined palms, holding up the water-pot.
Having learned of his wife’s infidelity, the sage became enraged and said, "O sons, kill this sinful woman! Though thus addressed, they did not do so.
Urged by his father, Rāma killed her along with his brother and their mother.
Knowing fully the power of the sage’s perfect meditative absorption and asceticism,
the son of Satyavatī, being pleased, invited him to choose a boon;
Rāma also chose the restoration to life of those who had been slain, provided they lacked memory of their slaughter.
They rose up at once, as if their sleep had been dispelled, and were restored to health;

O King, the wise Rāma, remembering the slaughter of his father, performed a penance of such power that he brought about the death of his kinsmen. Those sons of Arjuna, O King, remained there constantly mindful of the slaying of their own father.
Defeated by the prowess of Rāma, they found no peace anywhere.
Once, when Rāma had gone from his hermitage to the forest with his brothers,
those enemies, seeking to avenge their enmity, approached him having found an opportunity.
Seeing the sage seated in the fire-sanctuary with his mind absorbed in the Blessed One, the Lord of Excellent Renown, those men of evil intent struck him down,
despite being entreated by Rāma’s mother with piteous cries. They were exceedingly cruel.

Having forcibly cut off his head, those base kṣatriyas carried it away; then Reṇukā, afflicted by pain and grief, began to strike herself with her own hand, while that virtuous woman cried out loudly, "Rāma! Rāma! Father!"
Hearing that sound from afar, crying out "Alas, Rāma!
like those in agony, they quickly reached the hermitage and saw their father slain.
Overwhelmed by the force of grief, delusion, and the pain of sorrow, anger, and resentment, they were utterly distraught.
"Alas, dear father! O virtuous one, most righteous! Having abandoned us, you have gone to heaven.
Having lamented thus and entrusted his father’s body to his brothers, Rāma himself took up an axe and set his mind upon the destruction of the Kṣatriyas.
Having gone to Māhiṣmatī, whose prosperity had been destroyed by those slayers of Brahmins, O King, Rāma placed their heads in the midst of a great mountain; with their blood,
he created a terrible river that brought fear to those who were hostile to Brahmanas.
Making the slaughter of his father the pretext,
the Lord, having cleared the earth of the Kṣatriya caste twenty-one times from that inauspicious race,
created nine lakes of blood at Samantapañcaka.
Having joined his head with the body of his father and placed it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), he worshipped the Lord—
who embodies all the gods— as his own self through sacrifices. He gave the eastern direction to the Hotṛ priest and the southern direction to the Brahman priest as sacrificial fees.
He gave the western direction to the Adhvaryu priest, the northern direction to the Udgātṛ priest,
the intermediate directions to the others, and the center to Kaśyapa; thereafter,
he gave Āryāvarta to the Upadraṣṭṛ and the Sadasyas.
Then, his every impurity shaken off by the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*),
he shone upon the great river Sarasvatī like the sun in a cloudless sky.
Jamadagni, having regained his own body, which was characterized by consciousness and life, [shone forth].
He became the seventh in the circle of the ṛṣis, honored by Rāma. O King,
the lotus-eyed Lord Rāma, the son of Jamadagni,
will indeed propagate the *Bṛhat* [Saṃhitā] in a future age.
Even today, he remains on Mount Mahendra, having laid down the rod of punishment, his mind perfectly tranquil,
while his deeds are sung by Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas.
Thus did the Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller and Soul of the universe, dwell among the Bhṛgus.
Having descended [to earth], he repeatedly slew many kings who were a heavy burden to the world.
Born as the son of Gādhi, he was possessed of great splendor like a kindled fire;
having renounced the duties of a Kṣatriya through ascetic penance, he attained the luster of Brahman.

O King, Viśvāmitra had one hundred and one sons; Madhucchandas was the middlemost among them, and his sons were those very ones. Having adopted Śunaḥśepha as a son, he [became] Devarāta, the descendant of Bhṛgu.

Ājīgarta said to his sons: "Let this eldest one be designated as the man who is to be sold as a sacrificial animal at Hariścandra’s sacrifice. Having praised the gods, headed by Prajeśa, he was released from his bonds.
He who was given by the gods at the place of sacrifice for the gods among the Gādhis,
the ascetic known as Devarāta, was Śunaḥśepha of the Bhṛgu lineage.
As for those sons of Madhucchandas, the eldest of whom did not consider that to be well done—
The sage, enraged, cursed them: "Become barbarians, O wicked ones!
Then Madhucchandas, together with fifty others, said:
"We shall abide by whatever you deem fit for us."
They made you, the seer of mantras, their eldest, for we were indeed following after you.
Viśvāmitra said to his sons: "You shall be possessed of heroes, you who, honoring my honor, have made me possessed of heroes."
O Kuśikas, this hero Devarāta is yours;
along with him are Aṣṭaka, Hārīta, Jaya, Kratu, Madu, and others.
Thus, the Kauśika lineage is divided into various branches by the Viśvāmitras.
Having entered another lineage, it was indeed thus ordained.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Purūravas had a son named Āyu, and he had sons.
Nahuṣa, Kṣatravṛddha, Raji, the heroic Rābha,
and Anenā— O king of kings, hear now the lineage of Kṣatravṛddha. Kṣatravṛddha’s son was Suhotra, who had three sons.
From Gṛtsamada were born Kāśya, Kuśa, and Gṛtsamada; from Gṛtsamada came Śunaka, whose son was the sage Śaunaka, the preeminent among the Bahvṛcas.
Kāśya’s son was Kāśi; his son was Rāṣṭra, the father of Dīrghatamas.
Dhanvantari, the founder of Ayurveda, was born from Dīrghatamas;
he is a portion of Vāsudeva, the enjoyer of sacrifice, who destroys all suffering upon being remembered.
His son was Ketumān, and from him was born Bhīmaratha.
From him [Divodāsa] came Dyumant, from whom Pratardana is remembered;
he himself was called Śatrujit, Vatsa, and Ṛtadhvaja; likewise, he was proclaimed as Kuvalayāśva, and from him came Alarka and others.
O King, for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years, no one other than Nala was a youth who enjoyed the earth;
from Alarka came his lineage: Sunītha, and then Niketana.

From him was born Dharmaketu; from him Satyaketu was born; from him Dhṛṣṭaketu; from him Sukumāra, the lord of the earth; his son was Vītihotra; from him came Bharga; and from him, O King, was born Bhārgabhūmi.
Thus these were the kings of the Kāśaya lineage, descendants of Kṣatravṛddha.
Rābhasya’s son was Rabhasa, and from him came Gambhīra and Akriya.
From that lineage was born Brahmavij; now hear the genealogy of Anenas.
From him was born Śuddha; from him, Śuci; from him, Citrakṛt, who was a charioteer of dharma.
From him was born Śāntarajas, who was self-possessed and had fulfilled his duties. Raji had five hundred sons of immeasurable splendor.
Requested by the gods, He slew the Daityas and restored heaven to Indra;
Indra, in turn, having returned it to Him, grasped the feet of Raji and offered himself up,
fearing that Prahlāda and others might seize the kingdom.
When their father had passed away, the sons did not give [the kingdom] to us who requested it;
they withheld the sacrificial portions from Mahendra for the sake of Triviṣṭapa.
While the preceptor was offering oblations into the fire, the slayer of Bala [Indra] seized the sons of Raji.
He slew those who had strayed from the path, leaving none remaining.
From Kuśa was born Prati; from Kṣātravṛddha came Sañjaya, and his son was Jaya.
From him was born Kṛta, and from Kṛta was born King Haryabala.
Sahadeva was inferior to him, and his son was Jayasena; his son was Saṅkṛti, whose son was Jaya, the great chariot-warrior Kṣatradharman.
These were the kings of the lineage of Kṣatravṛddha; now hear of the descendants of Nahuṣa.
Śrī Śuka said:
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, Viyati, and Kṛti—
these six were the sons of Nahuṣa, like the senses of an embodied being.
Knowing its ultimate consequence, the renunciant did not desire the kingdom offered by his father— a realm into which a man who enters no longer recognizes his own self—
after his father had been displaced from his station due to the assault of Indrāṇī and the machinations of the twice-born.
When he had indeed been reduced to the state of a python, King Yayāti appointed his younger brothers to the four quarters;
having taken wives, he protected the earth under the patronage of Kāvya Vṛṣaparvan.
The King said:
"How was there a marriage between the venerable Brahmarṣi Kāvya and the base Kṣatriya, the son of Nahuṣa? Why did this marriage occur in the reverse order between a Kṣatriya and a Brāhmaṇa?"
Śrī Śuka said:
Once, there was a daughter of the lord of the Dānavas named Śarmiṣṭhā,
a beautiful woman accompanied by a thousand female companions and the daughter of her preceptor.
In the city garden of Devayānī, crowded with trees in full bloom,
that frail woman wandered upon the sandy banks of the lotus pond where bees hummed sweet songs.
Having reached that reservoir, those lotus-eyed maidens—
Having set aside their fine silken garments on the bank, they were splashing one another;
but seeing Giriśa proceeding with the Goddess, seated upon his bull,
the women suddenly emerged from the water and, filled with shame, put on their clothes.
Not realizing it was the garment of her guru’s daughter, Śarmiṣṭhā wore it, thinking it was her own;
consequently, the enraged Devayānī spoke as follows:
"Alas! Behold this improper deed of this maidservant!"

Those by whom this [world] was created through austerity, who are the mouth of the Supreme Person, and by whom the light is sustained here and the auspicious path revealed; they have been held by you like a dog holding the sacrificial oblation at a sacrifice.
Those whom the lords of the worlds and the rulers of the gods salute and attend upon—
even the Blessed Lord himself, the soul of the universe, the purifier, and the abode of Śrī;
and even among them, we are the Bhṛgus, whose preceptor is our father, the Asura.
"Like an unchaste Śūdra woman who has taken up the Veda as something she ought to maintain, you have taken up what is to be maintained by us.
To Śarmiṣṭhā, who was thus reviling her, the daughter of the guru spoke,
hissing in rage like a trampled female serpent with its fangs bared.
"O beggar-woman, you boast much without knowing your own true nature!
Why do you not wait upon our houses like a crow for scraps?
Having thus insulted the virtuous daughter of the preceptor with such exceedingly harsh words, [the King departed].
Out of anger, Śarmiṣṭhā threw her into a well and took her garment;
when she had gone to her own home, Yayāti, while wandering on a hunt,
arrived at the well by chance seeking water and beheld her there.
Having given his own upper garment to her who was naked, the king,
devoted to compassion, took her hand in his own and raised her up.
Then the daughter of Uśanas addressed that hero with words overflowing with love.

"O King, conqueror of enemy cities, my hand has been taken by you; let there be no other grasping of the hand for me, now that I have been accepted by you. O Hero, this bond between us was ordained by the Lord; it is not a human creation."
That I have received this vision of you while submerged in a well—
O mighty-armed one, no Brāhmaṇa shall ever become my husband,
for I previously cursed Yama due to the curse of Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati.

Yayāti, perceiving that his own mind was set upon what was undesirable and brought about by fate, accepted those words. When the steadfast king had departed, she remained there weeping for her father.
Then he reported everything that had been done by Śarmiṣṭhā; thereupon,
the venerable son of Kavi (Śukrācārya), being dejected and censuring his office as priest while praising the lifestyle of a pigeon,
departed from the city with his daughter.
Recognizing that his preceptor intended to oppose him, Vṛṣaparvan prostrated himself at the teacher's feet on the road to appease him;
then the blessed descendant of Bhṛgu, his anger subsided for half a moment, spoke to his disciple.
"O King, let her desire be fulfilled; I do not venture to abandon her here. When he had agreed, saying "So be it," Devayānī spoke what was in her mind:
"Since she has been given away by my father, she shall go; let her follow me along with her attendants."
Then, having been given along with her attendants to Devayānī by her father, Śarmiṣṭhā—
seeing the distress of her own kin and the great weight of her master’s purpose—
served Devayānī like a maidservant, accompanied by a thousand women.
Having given his daughter to the son of Nahuṣa along with Śarmiṣṭhā, Uśanas said to him,
"O King, never place Śarmiṣṭhā upon the bed. O King, having observed at some time that Śarmiṣṭhā had given birth to noble offspring, [Uśanas spoke].

When her husband died, that virtuous woman chose him alone as her companion in secret; and though requested by the princess for the sake of offspring, he— who was a knower of dharma— considered both dharma and the words of Śukra, and remembering them, submitted at the proper time to what was ordained by destiny.
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu,
while Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, gave birth to Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.
Having learned from her husband that the conception of the children was due to Āsuri, the proud Devayānī [became resentful].
Devayānī departed for her father’s house, overwhelmed with anger.
Following after his beloved, the lustful king attempted to conciliate her with words and by massaging her feet and other such services, but he was unable to appease her.

Śukra, enraged by that man who had lied out of lust for a woman, said to him: "O dull-witted one, may old age, which causes deformity in men, enter you! To this, Yayāti replied: *The Blessed Śukra said:* "O dull-witted one, may old age, which causes deformity in men, enter you! *Yayāti said:* "I am old, O Brahmin; my senses have failed me. My youth has departed, and I am unable to enjoy the pleasures of the senses."

"I am not yet satiated with desires regarding your daughter, O Brahmin; let her be given as she wishes to whoever shall surpass me in age. Having thus established the condition, he spoke to his eldest son.
"O dear one, Yadu, accept this old age of mine and give me back your own youth;
my child, I am not yet satiated with sense objects. With your age, I shall enjoy myself for some years."
Śrī Yadu said:
"I do not venture to remain here while you have already reached old age;
for a person does not attain freedom from desire without first experiencing the pleasures of worldly life."
O descendant of Bharata, Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu, being urged by their father, refused [to take charge],
for they were ignorant of dharma and possessed the notion of permanence regarding that which is impermanent.
He then questioned his son Pūru, who was superior in virtue and not yet old in years.
"But, my child, you ought not to reject me as your elder brother did.
Śrī Puru said:
"O lord of men, what man in this world can truly act against the will of his father?"
He who, by the grace of another, attains the supreme goal is capable of returning that favor;

he who performs what was intended is excellent, while one who merely carries out what was commanded is mediocre; the inferior son performs the father’s command without faith, and the lowest does not perform it at all.
Thus delighted, Pūru accepted his father’s old age; and he, O King, enjoyed all desires as was fitting through that [father’s] age,
while ruling the seven islands properly like a father, protecting his subjects.

With his senses unimpaired, he enjoyed sense objects according to his pleasure; and Devayānī, the beloved wife, likewise brought the highest delight to her lover day after day through her mind, speech, body, and material offerings in private.

He worshipped Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, who embodies all the gods and all the Vedas, with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees; in Him this entire universe is fashioned, like a row of clouds in the sky.
Like a dream, an illusion, or a mental fantasy, it appears as manifold and yet does not truly appear;
having placed that very Vāsudeva, who dwells in the secret cave of the heart, within his own heart—
that Lord Nārāyaṇa, more subtle than the atom— he performed sacrifice without any desire for rewards.
Thus, for thousands of years, although that sovereign of the whole earth provided mental pleasure through the six senses, he was not satisfied by his wretched organs. Śrī Śuka said:
Acting thus, he who was devoted to women, having realized his own self-deception regarding desires,
became despondent with his beloved and sang this verse:
"O daughter of Bhṛgu, listen to this verse concerning my conduct on earth."
Even the wise who dwell in the forest grieve for him who lives in a village;
like a certain goat searching for his own beloved in the forest,
he saw a she-goat fallen into a well, brought there by the power of her own karma.
Reflecting upon the means to rescue her, the lustful goat dug out a path with the tip of his horns between the two banks of the river;
having crossed over from the well, that woman of beautiful hips indeed fell in love with him alone.
Seeing him chosen by her— fat, bearded, most beloved, bountiful, and skilled in the ways of women— many other goats, longing for their lover,
[approached]. That single buck-goat increased the pleasure of those many females.
Seized by the demon of lust, he took his pleasure and did not perceive his own true self.
Seeing him sporting with that other woman who was most dear to him, the cow, agitated as if by a well, could not endure that act of her husband.

Abandoning that master— who was a wicked-hearted man in the guise of a friend, a lustful seeker of momentary affection, and one who delighted only in the objects of the senses— the distressed woman departed. He too, being devoted to women and wretched, followed after her to propitiate her.
Making a "ḍaviḍā" sound, he was unable to proceed on the road;
there, a certain brahmin named Ajāsvāmin, an expert in yoga, angrily cut off his dangling testicles and then reattached them for his benefit.
O blessed lady, even he whose testicles were joined together by Ajā, whom he had found in a well,
did not find satisfaction through his desires for many long years;
likewise, O fair-browed one, I am a wretch, constrained by my love for you.

Deluded by Your illusory power, I do not recognize my true self. For one like you, who is struck down by desire, rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women on this earth do not produce even a glimmer of satisfaction for the mind.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it increases all the more.
When one no longer harbors ill-will toward any living being, [then desire ceases].
For that man who possesses equal vision toward all, all directions are then filled with happiness; therefore,

one who desires well-being should quickly abandon that thirst for worldly objects— which is difficult for the foolish to relinquish even as they age, which does not itself age, and which brings forth a multitude of sufferings.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a wise man.
Although I have repeatedly indulged in sense objects for a full thousand years, [I have still not attained satisfaction].
Nevertheless, thirst for them arises in me at every moment;
therefore, having abandoned this [desire], I shall fix my mind upon Brahman,
and free from dualities and egoism, I shall wander with the deer.
"Having understood that what is seen and heard is unreal, one should not dwell upon it nor give instructions regarding it;
for therein lies both worldly existence and the destruction of the self—he who knows this is a seer of the Self.
Having spoken thus to his wife, the son of Nahuṣa transferred his own youth to Pūru.
Having given his own old age to him, he, free from desire, took it back again.
He appointed Druhyu as ruler over the southeast, Yadu over the south, Turvasu over the west, and Anu as lord over the north.

Having consecrated Pūru, the most worthy among the people, as the sovereign over the entire circle of the earth, and having established his elder brothers under his authority, he departed for the forest. There,
for many series of years, he practiced mastery over the six internal enemies regarding the objects of the senses.
In an instant, he abandoned his nest like a bird whose wings have grown;

there, having cast off all attachments and shaken off the three marks of material nature through the realization of the Self, he, being fully enlightened, attained the supreme state of devotion in the stainless Brahman, Vāsudeva.
Having heard this verse, Devayānī considered it to be a mockery directed at herself,
uttered like a jest arising from the emotional agitation of affection between a man and a woman—
just as one might mock friends who are departing for a watering hole.
Having understood that everything created by Māyā belongs to the Lord who is the master of all,
and having abandoned attachment to everything— viewing it as being like a dream— the daughter of Bhṛgu fixed her mind on Kṛṣṇa and shook off her subtle body.
"Obeisances to You, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Creator;
obeisances to the Great Peace who dwells within all beings.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
I shall proclaim the lineage of Pūru, in which you were born, O Bhārata;
in which royal sages and those of the brahminical lineage were born as its descendants. Janamejaya was the son of Pūru, and from him came his son Pracinvān.
From Manu came Pravīra, and from him was born Cārupada.
His son was Sudyu; from him came Bahugava.
Saṃyāti was his son, and Ahaṃyāti is recorded as his son; Raudrāśva was known as the son of the latter.
Ṛteyu, Kakṣeyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, Kṛteyuka,
Jaleyu, Sannateyu, Dharmeyu, Satyeyu, and Vrateyu—
these ten were the sons of Apsaras; Vaneyu is recorded as the youngest.
From Ghṛtācī was born Ṛteyu, who was like the senses of the Chief One, the Soul of the Universe;
his sons were Rantināva, Sumati, Dhruva, and Apratiratha, O King; and Kaṇva was the son of Apratiratha.
From him [Medhātithi] was born Medhātithi; from him were born the twice-born Praskanna and others.
Sumati’s son was Rebha, and his son is considered to be Duṣmanta. Having gone out on a hunt, Duṣmanta arrived at the hermitage of Kaṇva.
Seeing her seated there, adorning [the place] with her own radiance like the goddess Ramā, he was instantly bewildered by that woman who was like the illusory power (*māyā*) of the gods;
surrounded by a few soldiers, he addressed that woman of beautiful hips.
Delighted by the sight of her, his fatigue dispelled yet tormented by desire, he asked with a smile and in gentle words:
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? Whose beloved heart-captivating woman are you?"
"What do you intend to do there in this desolate forest?
Clearly, O slender-waisted one, I know you to be the daughter of a royal prince;
for the heart of the Pauravas never finds pleasure in unrighteousness."
Śrī Śakuntalā said: "O hero, I am the daughter of Viśvāmitra, abandoned by Menakā in the forest; the venerable Kaṇva knows this. What may I do for you?"
"O lotus-eyed one, please be seated; accept our hospitality.
Please eat, for there is wild rice here; stay, if it pleases you.
Thus spoke Śrī Duṣmanta.
"O fair-browed one, this is fitting for you, born as you are in the lineage of Kuśika;
for daughters of kings choose a husband of their own accord who is their equal. When she had said "So be it," he married Śakuntalā according to the sacred law.

The royal sage Amoghavīrya, a king who knew the proper rules regarding place and time, bestowed his seed upon the queen according to the Gāndharva rite; having departed for his own city on the following day, she gave birth to a son in due course of time.
Kaṇva performed the appropriate rites for the boy in the forest;
that child, having quickly bound the king of beasts, played with him. Taking him, whose prowess was difficult to overcome, the most excellent woman [Yaśodā]—

When the king did not accept his blameless wife and son— who had been born from a portion of a portion of Hari— then, as all living beings listened, an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky: "When the king did not accept his blameless wife and son— who had been born from a portion of a portion of Hari— he approached the presence of his husband."
"The mother is but a leather bag; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very one by whom he was begotten.
Support your son, O Duṣmanta; do not despise Śakuntalā.
O King, the son who bears the seed leads his progenitor from the abode of Yama."
And you are the sustainer of this embryo; Śakuntalā spoke the truth.
When his father has passed away, he too will be a world-renowned universal emperor (cakravartin), and the greatness of him, who is born from a portion of Hari, shall be sung upon the earth.
A discus was on his right hand and a lotus bud was on his feet;
having been consecrated with the great royal ablution, that all-pervading sovereign became the supreme ruler.
He performed sacrifices along the Ganges with fifty-five pure horses.
Placing the son of Mamatā at the head of his priestly retinue, the Lord [Saudāsa] bound seventy-eight sacrificial horses along the Yamunā while bestowing wealth;
for Agni had been piled up by Bharata, the son of Duṣmanta, as a witness to his virtues.
In that sacrifice, thousands upon thousands of Brahmins divided the cows;
having bound three thousand three hundred horses,
the son of Duṣmanta surpassed the illusions of others and attained the supreme illusion of the gods.
At the Maṣṇāra sacrifice, he gave fourteen million black antelopes with white teeth, encased in gold;
such was the great deed of Bharata, which neither kings of the past nor those of the future have equaled.
Just as they could not reach heaven with their own two arms,
so too [the Lord] struck down the Kirātas, Hūṇas, Yavanas, Pauṇḍras, Kaṅkas, Khaśas, Śakas,
and all the Mleccha kings who were hostile to the Brahmanas during his conquest of the quarters.
In former times, having conquered the gods, the Asuras took possession of the subterranean abodes (rasaukāṃsi).
When the celestial women were carried away to Rasātala by those creatures, he recovered them once again.
For him, heaven and earth (rodasī) milked forth all the objects of desire for his subjects.
For twenty-seven thousand years, he set his wheel in motion in all directions.
As the sovereign overlord, he attained the sovereignty known as that of the world-protectors, as well as prosperity;
yet, regarding the wheel and his very life-breaths as insignificant, he eventually desisted.
O King, he had three highly esteemed wives from Vidarbha.

When it was said that their sons were not worthy [of his lineage], they killed them out of fear of being abandoned. Thus, when his lineage remained fruitless, he performed sacrifices for the sake of obtaining a son.

By means of the Marutstoma sacrifice, the Maruts obtained Bharadvāja. Bṛhaspati, having approached his brother’s pregnant wife for sexual union, was forbidden; yet, after cursing her womb, he discharged his semen.
To her who desired to abandon him and was apprehensive about her husband’s desertion, the gods sang this verse explaining his name:
“O deluded woman, support this son of Dvija; support the son of Dvija, O Bṛhaspati!”
After his parents had departed having spoken thus, Bharadvāja was then exhorted by the gods; realizing that his son was indeed futile,
he released the Maruts, saying, "This Datta has been born into a lineage that is fruitless."
Śrī Śuka said:
The sons of Manyu, the son of Vitatha, were Bṛhatkṣatra, Jaya, Mahāvīrya, Nara, Garga, and Saṅkṛti; Nara was the father of Saṅkṛti.
O son of Pāṇḍu, both Guru and Rantideva were disciples of Saṅkṛti;
the greatness of Rantideva is sung of both in this world and the next,
as he gave away whatever wealth he obtained while desiring to enjoy it.
For forty-eight days, it is said, the wise man— who was destitute of possessions yet maintained his family— passed his time without drinking,
even though ghee, milk-rice, wheat-cakes, and water were presented to him every morning.
To him whose family had fallen into distress, who was trembling with hunger and thirst,
and who desired to eat at the proper time, a guest— a brāhmaṇa— arrived;
he, full of respect and endowed with faith, shared his food with him.

Seeing Hari everywhere, that twice-born man ate and departed. Then, O King, another man, remembering Hari, gave a portion of the food intended for the king— who was about to eat his own share— to that outcaste.
When the Śūdra had departed, another guest arrived, surrounded by dogs, and said:
"O King, let food be given to me and my retinue, for we are hungry. Taking great care and honoring him with respect, he gave him what remained.
Having given that, the powerful one bowed down to the dogs and to the Lord of Dogs; there remained only a small amount of water, sufficient for a single libation,
which he was about to drink when a Pulkasa approached and said, "Give water to me for my purification."
Having heard those words of his, which were full of compassion and born of great exhaustion,
the Lord, deeply moved by pity, spoke these nectar-like words:
"I do not desire from the Lord a supreme goal endowed with the eight mystic powers, nor even liberation from rebirth."

I take refuge in Him who, dwelling within all embodied beings, causes them to be free from suffering. Through the offering of the water of life by Me, all the hunger, thirst, fatigue, bodily exhaustion, wretchedness, weariness, grief, despair, and delusion of this miserable creature who desires to live have entirely ceased.

Having spoken thus, O King, the wise monarch, whose very nature was compassion, as he was dying of thirst, offered water to the Pulkasī woman. To those who desire fruits, the lords of the three worlds are the granters of those fruits.
They manifested themselves through illusions created by Viṣṇu.
Having offered obeisances to them, he— free from attachment and devoid of desire—
directed his mind with supreme devotion toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
O King, for him who made his mind rest upon the Lord and whose success depended on no other means, the illusory energy composed of the modes of nature dissolved like a dream.
By the power of that constant association, even those following Rantideva [were similarly transformed].
All those yogīs became solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
From Garga came Śini, from whom Gārgya was born; for from that Kṣatriya, the Brahmanhood indeed emerged.
From Duritakṣaya, who was of great prowess, were born Trayyāruṇi and the sage Kavi.

Among those who attained the status of Brahmins, such as Puṣkarāruṇi and others, Hastī was born as the son of Bṛhatkṣatra; from him came Hastināpura. Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and Purumīḍha were the sons of Hastī.
The descendants of Ajamīḍha were the twice-born priests beginning with Priyamedha.
From Ajamīḍha was born Bṛhadiṣu; his son was Bṛhaddhanu;
from him came Bṛhatkāya, and his son was Jayadratha.
His son was Viśada, from whom Syenajit was born.
Rucirāśva, Dṛḍhahanu, Kāśya, and Vatsa were his sons. Pāra was the son of Rucirāśva, and Pṛthusena was his offspring.
Pāra’s son was Nīpa, who had one hundred sons.
He begot Brahmadatta upon Kṛtvī, the daughter of Śuka;
that yogi fathered Viṣvaksena as a son upon his wife Gavi.
Through the instruction of Jaigīṣavya, Udakasena indeed composed a treatise on Yoga; from him came Bhallāṭa, and then the Bārhadīṣavas.
Yavīnara was the son of Dvimīḍha, and Kṛtimān is recorded as his son.
His son was Satyadhṛti by name; his son was Dṛḍhanemi, who begot Supārśva. From Supārśva came Sumati, and from him Sannatimān.
His son was Kṛtī, the son of Hiraṇyanābha, who, having attained yoga, sang the *Ṣaṭpada*.
From him came Saṃhitā, the son of Prācyasāman; from him came Nīpa, whose weapon was raised high.
His son was Kṣemya; then Suvīra; and from Suvīra came Ripuñjaya.
From him came the one named Bahuratha; Purumīḍha was childless.
From Nalinyā, the son of Ajamīḍha was Nīla; Śānti was his son.
Suśānti was the son of Śānti, and from him Puru was born, whose son was Arka. Bharmyāśva was his son, and he had five sons, Mudgala and the others.

Yavīnara, Bṛhadviśva, Kāmpilla, Sañjaya, and Bharmyāśva were the sons [of Divodāsa]. He said, "These five are indeed sufficient for the protection of the five regions"; thus they were known as the Pañcālas.

From Mudgala originated the lineage known as Maudgalya, which was established by a Brahmin. From Mudgala and his wife Bhāryā a pair of children was born: the male child was Divodāsa, and the female child was Ahalyā, from whom Śatānanda was born through Gautama.
His son was Satyadhṛti, who was highly skilled in the science of archery;
his son was Śaradvat, from whom, it is said, a pair of children emerged as a beautiful couple when his semen fell into a clump of reeds upon seeing Urvaśī.
Seeing that, Śāntanu, while out hunting, took them out of compassion;
Kṛpa became the prince, and the girl became Kṛpī, the wife of Droṇa.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, from Divodāsa was born Mitrāyu; his son was Cyavana. From Sudāsa came Sahadeva, and then Somaka, the progenitor of Jantu.
He had a hundred sons, among whom the youngest was Pṛṣata.
From him was born Drupada, endowed with every prosperity.
From Drupada came Draupadī, and his sons were Dhṛṣṭadyumna and others. From Dhṛṣṭadyumna came Dhṛṣṭaketu; these are the descendants of Pāñcāla through Bhāryā.
The son of Ajamīḍha was another, Ṛkṣa; from him came Saṃvaraṇa, and from him, through Tapatī, the daughter of the Sun, came Kuru, the lord of Kurukṣetra.
Parīkṣit, Sudhanus, Jahnu, and Niṣadha were the sons of Kuru.
From Sudhanus was born Suhotra; from him came Cyavana, and from him Kṛtī.
His son was Vasu, whose son was Uparicara, followed by Bṛhadratha and others.
From him descended Kuśāmba, Matsya, Pratyagra, Cedipa, and other kings of Cedi.
From Bṛhadratha was born Kuśāgra; his son was Ṛṣabha. From him was born Satyahita as offspring, and Puṣpavān was his son. From Bṛhadratha, by another wife, two fragments (śakale) were born.
When the mother cast him outside and he was touched by old age,
she played with him, saying "Live, O Jīva," and thus Jarāsaṃdha became his son;
from him Sahadeva was born, who was also known as Somāpi and Śrutaśravas.
Parīkṣit was childless; his son was named Suratha, who was descended from Jahnu.
From him came Vidūratha, and from him Sārvabhauma was born. Jayasena was his son, from whom Rādhika was born, and from him Ayutāyu arose.
From him was born Akrodhana; from that deity came Devātithi, and his son was Ṛkṣa. Dilīpa was born from him, and Pratīpa was his son. Devāpi, Śāntanu, and Bāhlīka were his sons.
Having renounced his paternal kingdom, Devāpi went to the forest.
Formerly, there was a king named Mahābhiṣa who became Śāntanu;
whomever he touched with his two hands, that person, though aged, attained youth.

And by that deed, Śāntanu attained the highest peace. When the Lord did not send rain for twelve years during his reign, Śāntanu was told by the brāhmaṇas: "This man is a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother) and an *agrabhuj* (one who eats first)."
"Give the kingdom quickly to your elder brother for the prosperity of the city and the realm.
Thus addressed by the twice-born, he invited his eldest brother [to accept], but the latter spoke,
having been led astray from the Veda by the words of the brahmins sent by that minister.
At that time, the Lord indeed rained down the supreme declarations of the Vedas. Devāpi, having resorted to yoga, took refuge in the village of Kalāpa;
when the Lunar dynasty has perished in the Kali age, he will re-establish it at the beginning of the Kṛta age.
From Bāhlīka was born Somadatta, and from him came Bhūri and Bhūriśravas. From Śāntanu, by Gaṅgā, was born the self-controlled Bhīṣma,
the best among those who know all dharmas, a great devotee of the Lord, and a seer.
By him, the leader of the hosts of heroes, even Rāma was gratified in battle;
from Śāntanu and the daughter of the Dāsa, a son named Citrāṅgada was born. Vicitravīrya was his younger brother, and Citrāṅgada was slain.
In her, from Parāśara himself, descended a portion of Hari,
the sage Vedavyāsa Kṛṣṇa, from whom I learned this [Veda],
after the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa had left behind his own disciples, Paila and the others.

To me, his peaceful son, Vicitravīrya sang this supreme secret; then he spoke regarding both Ambikā and Ambālikā, the two daughters of the King of Kāśī, who had been brought by force from their *svayaṃvara*.
With his heart attached to those two, he was seized by consumption and died; then,
at the command of his mother, Bādarāyaṇa begot Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura in the field of his childless brother.
O King, from Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī were born one hundred sons;
among them, Duryodhana was the eldest, and there was also a daughter named Duḥśalā.
Furthermore, due to a curse that had obstructed his sexual union, Pāṇḍu begot great chariot-warriors upon Kuntī.
From Dharma, Vāyu, and Indra were born three sons headed by Yudhiṣṭhira;
Nakula and Sahadeva were born from Mādrī by the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas.
From Draupadī, five sons were born from these five fathers, and they became their progenitors.
From Yudhiṣṭhira was born Prativindhya; from Vṛkodara, Śrutasena;
from Arjuna, Śrutakīrti; and Śatānīka was the son of Nakula. O King, Sahadeva’s son was Śrutakarman, as well as others.
From Yudhiṣṭhira and Pauravī were born Devaka and Ghaṭotkaca;
from Bhīmasena and Hiḍimbā was born Sarvagata;
and from Sahadeva and Vijayā, Pārvatī gave birth to Suhotra.
From Kareṇumatī, Nakula had Naramitra, and likewise Arjuna had Irāvanta from Ulūpī;
and Babhruvāhana was born from his daughter,
who was the son of the lord of Maṇipura through a putrikā marriage.
Your father Abhimanyu was born of Subhadrā;

he was a hero who conquered all great chariot-warriors (atirathas). From him, you were born of Uttarā, after the Kurus had been utterly destroyed by the fiery power of the Brahmāstra weapon of Aśvatthāman.
And you, O dear one, were restored to life from the jaws of death by the power of Kṛṣṇa;
these are your sons, headed by Janamejaya—
Śrutasena, Bhīmasena, and the heroic Ugrasena.
Janamejaya, having learned that Takṣaka has met his death at your hands,
will— filled with rage and placing the son of Kaliṅga at his head as his priest— offer the serpents into the fire of the snake-sacrifice, he who is a conqueror of even the horse-sacrifice.
Having conquered the entire earth on all sides, he will perform sacrifices with ritual offerings.
His son, Śatānīka, while studying the three Vedas from Yājñavalkya,
will attain mastery of the science of weapons and the science of ritual action from Śaunaka.
His son will be Sahasrānīka, and from him shall come Aśvamedhaja;
his son will be Asīmakṛṣṇa, and his son will be Nemicakra.
When the city called Gajāhvaya is swept away by a river, he will dwell virtuously in Kauśāmbī.
From him was born Citraratha; from him, his son Śuciratha; from him, Vṛṣṭimat; from him, King Suṣeṇa; his son will be Sunītha; [then] Nṛcakṣus, and then Sukhīnala.
From him [Bṛhatkṣatra] was born Pariplava; his son was Medhāvī, the son of Sunaya.
From him came Nṛpañjaya, then Dūrva, and from him Timi will be born. From Timi came Bṛhadratha, and from him Śatānīka, the son of Sudāsa.
From Śatānīka shall come Durdamana, and his offspring shall be Mahīnara; from him shall come Daṇḍapāṇi, then Nimi, and from him Kṣemaka,
from whom this lineage— the source of both Brahmanas and Kshatriyas— honored by divine sages, shall arise.
Having reached King Kṣemaka, he will indeed meet his end in the Kali age. Now, I shall describe those future kings of Magadha: from Sahadeva there will be Mārjāri, and [his son] Śrutaśravas.
From him will come Yutāyu; his son will be Niramitra, and his son Sunakṣatra; from Sunakṣatra will come Bṛhatsena, then Karmajit;
from Sutañjaya will come Vipra, and Śuci will be his son.
From him [Kṛtavīrya] came Kṣema, then Suvrata; from him, Dharmasūtra was born in his entirety.
Then came Dyumatsena, Sumati, and Subala, who was the father [of Rāma].
From him came Sunītha, then Satyajit, Viśvajit, and Ripuñjaya.
And the Bārhadratha kings shall rule for a thousand years.
Śrī Śuka said:
Anu had three sons: Sabhānara, Cakṣu, and Pareṣṇu.
From Sabhānara came Kālanara; his son was Sṛñjaya. From him came Janamejaya, whose sons were Mahāśāla and the high-minded Mahāmanas.
Uśīnara and Titikṣu were the two sons of Mahāmanas.
Śibirvara, Kṛmi, Dakṣa, and Catvāra were the sons of Aśīnara; Vṛṣādarbha, Sudhīra, Madra, and the self-controlled Kekaya were the sons of Śibi; and Titikṣu had Ruṣadratha as his son.
From him was born Homa; from Homa was born Sutapas; and from Sutapas was born Bali.

From Bali, the lord of the earth, were born in the womb of his wife the kings known as Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and others, as well as those named Suhma, Puṇḍra, and Oḍra, all of whom were born of Dīrghatamas.

They established these six regions and the eastern territories under their own names. Khalapāna was born from Aṅga; from him came Diviratha, whose son was Dharmaratha, and from him was born Citraratha, who was childless.
To him, known as Romapāda, his friend Daśaratha gave his own daughter Śāntā, whom Ṛṣyaśṛṅga married;
he was the son of a doe whom the Rāma queens had brought when the god did not send rain.
With dances, songs, instrumental music, playful gestures, embraces, and offerings,
he performed a sacrifice for the childless king Marutta;
by that sacrifice, Daśaratha, who was previously childless, obtained offspring.
From Romapāda came Caturaṅga, and his son was Pṛthulākṣa;
Bṛhadratha, Bṛhatkarman, and Bṛhadbhānu were his sons.
From the first of these came Bṛhanmanas, and from him Jayadratha is said to have descended.
From his wife Sambhūti was born Vijaya; from him was born Dhṛti;
from him, Dhṛtavrata; and from him, Satkarmā, also known as Adhiratha. It was he who, while playing on the banks of the Gaṅgā, [found] the infant within the basket.
O lord of the earth, being childless, Kuntī adopted as her son Vṛṣasena, who was born out of wedlock to Karṇa and had been cast away by her. Vṛṣasena was the son of Karṇa.
And the son of Druhyu was Babhru; from him came Setu as his offspring.
Ārabdha was his son; his son was Dharma, from whom Dhṛta was born.
From Dhṛta came Durmada, and from him was born Pracetā, who had one hundred sons known as the Prācetasas. These became lords of the Mlecchas, taking refuge in the northern direction.
The son of Turvasu was Vahni; from Vahni came Bharga, and then Bhānumat. His son was Tribhānu, and his son was the noble-minded Karandhama.
Marutta was his son; being childless, he adopted a descendant of Puru as his son.
O bull among men, Duṣmanta, desiring the kingdom, returned once more to his own lineage;
I shall now describe the lineage of Yadu, the eldest son of Yayāti, which is highly meritorious and removes all the sins of human beings.
A person who hears of Yadu’s lineage is liberated from all sins;
it was there that the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Self, descended in human form.
Among the descendants of Yadu, Sahasrajit, Kroṣṭā, Nala, and Ripu are well known.
He had four sons there; Śatajit was the first-born, and his sons were Mahāhaya, Reṇuhaya, and Haihaya. Dharmas, however, was the son of Haihaya, and from him came Netra, the father of Kunti.
Sohamjira was born as Kunteru, Mahiṣmān, and Bhadrasenaka;
Durmada was the son of Bhadrasena, and Dhanaka was the father of Kṛtavīrya; Kṛtāgni, Kṛtavarmā, and Kṛtaujas were the sons of Dhanaka.
Arjuna became the lord of the seven islands;
having obtained the great qualities of yoga from Dattātreya, who was a portion of Hari,
the kings will surely not attain the destiny of Kārtavīrya.
Through sacrifices, charity, austerity, yoga, sacred learning, valor, compassion, and other virtues, he—
possessing unimpeded strength and never losing his memory of wealth— enjoyed inexhaustible sixfold prosperity for eighty-five thousand years.
Of his thousand sons, only five remained in the battle:
Jayadhvaja, Śūrasena, Vṛṣabha, Madhu, and Ūrjita.
From Jayadhvaja was born Tālajaṅgha, who had a hundred sons.
The warrior class known as the Tālajaṅghas was annihilated by the fiery energy of Aurva.
Among them, Vītihotra was the eldest; he is remembered as the son of Madhu, from whom the lineage of Vṛṣṇi arose.
He had one hundred sons, of whom Vṛṣṇi was the eldest, from whom the family descended.
O King, they were known as the Mādhavas, the Vṛṣṇis, and the Yādavas. From Kroṣṭu, the son of Yadu, was born Vṛjinavat; from him came Svāhita; from him, Viṣadgu; and from him, Citraratha.
Śaśabindu became a great yogi, highly fortunate and exalted;
he was an unconquered universal monarch (cakravartin) possessing the fourteen great jewels. That man of immense fame had ten thousand wives.
He begot ten million sons through them;
among those, Pṛthuśravas was the son of six principal ones. His son was named Dharma, who was Uśanas, the performer of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
His son was Rucaka; listen now to his five sons who were born to him:
Purujit, Rukma, Rukmeṣu, Pṛthu, and the one named Jyāmagha.
Although Jyāmagha was childless, the husband of Śaibyā, out of fear, [approached] another wife.
He did not find a maiden suitable for marriage among the enemies' dwellings, so he abducted her while she was seated in a chariot.
Seeing her there, Śaibyā, filled with indignation, said to her husband:
"O deceiver, who is this woman that you have placed upon my chariot?"
When it was said, "She is your daughter-in-law," she smiled and said to her husband:
"I am barren and without co-wives; how can she be my daughter-in-law? O Queen, she is suitable for the son whom you shall father."
All the gods and the ancestors rejoiced at that;
Śaibyā conceived a fetus and in due time gave birth to an auspicious boy. He was called Vidarbha, and he married Satī as his daughter-in-law.
Śrī Śuka said:
Upon her, Vidarbha begot two sons named Kuśa and Kratha,
and a third, Romapāda, who brought joy to the lineage of Vidarbha.
Romapāda’s son was Babhru; from Babhru, Kṛti was born. Uśika was his son, and from him came Cedi and the kings such as Caidya. Kratha’s son was Kunti; his son was Vṛṣṇi, and his was Nirvṛti.
From him was born Daśārha by name; his son was Vyoma, from whom came Jīmūta; his son was Vikṛti, whose son was Bhīmaratha; from him was born Navaratha as a son, and from him, Daśaratha.
Karambhi was the son of Śakuni, and his son was Devarāta. From him came Devakṣatra; his sons were Madhu, Kuruvaśa, and Anu.
Puruhotra was the son of Anu, and from him came Āyu and Sātvata.
Bhajamāna, Bhaji, Divya, Vṛṣṇi, Devāvṛdha, Andhaka,
and Mahābhoja— these were the seven sons of Sātvata, O noble one. The sons of Bhajamāna were Nimloci, Kiṅkaṇa, and Dhṛṣṭi.
O Lord, from one wife he had one son, and from the other three sons named Śatājit, Sahasrājit, and Ayutājit; and Babhru was the son of Devāvṛdha. Regarding these two, people recite these verses:
Just as we hear him from afar, so do we behold him when near;
he is tawny-hued, the best among men, equal to the gods who increase the glory of the gods.
There were eight thousand, six hundred, and sixty-five men [who followed him].
Those who attained immortality even from Babhru Devāvṛdha were the Mahābhojas; among them was the exceedingly righteous Atidharmātman, and in his lineage were the Bhojas.
Vṛṣṇi’s son was Sumitra, and Yudhājit, the scorcher of foes, was also born of him.
Śini was the son of Anamitra, and from Anamitra came Nighna.
Prasena and Satrājit were the two sons of Nighna. The other son of Anamitra was Śini, and his son was Satyaka.
Yuyudhāna was Sātyaki; his son was Jaya, and from him came Kuṇi.
Yugandhara was the son of Anamitra, and Vṛṣṇi was another son after him.
From Śvaphalka, Citraratha and [Akrūra] were born of Gāndinī. And from Śvaphalka [there was Akrūra].
He had twelve renowned sons, headed by Akrūra:
Āsaṅga, Sārameya, Mṛduras, Mṛduvid, Giri, Dharmavṛddha, Sukarman, Kṣetropekṣa, and Arimardana.
Śatrughna, Gandhamāda, and Pratibāhu were the twelve;
their sister was named Sucārā, as were the two sons of Akrūra.
Likewise, Devavān and Upadeva were the sons of Citraratha.
Pṛthu, Vidūratha, and many other descendants of Vṛṣṇi; Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śuci, and Kambalabarhiṣa;
the son of Kukura was Vahni, and from him was born Vilomā.
Kapotaroman was his son, and Tumburu was his friend.
From Andhaka came Dundubhi; from him were born Avidyota and Punarvasu.
Ahuka and Ahuki were the two children born of Ahuka, and Ahuki was a daughter.
Devaka and Ugrasena were the two [husbands], and Devaka had four sons:
Devavān, Upadeva, Sudeva, and Devavardhana. O King, they had seven sisters, headed by Dhṛtadevā.
Vasudeva married Śāntidevā, Upadevā, Śrīdevā, Devarakṣitā,
Sahadevā, and Devakī. Kaṃsa, Sunāman, Nyagrodha, Kaṅka, Śaṅku, and Suhū were [his sons].
Then Rāṣṭrapāla and Dhṛṣṭi, the son of Ugrasena, were filled with joy;
as were Kaṃsā, Kaṃsavatī, Kaṅkā, Śūrabhū, and Rāṣṭrapālikā—
the daughters of Ugrasena and the wives of Vasudeva’s younger brothers.
Śūra was born from Vidūratha, and his son was Bhajamāna. From him came Śini; he himself was a Bhoja, and Hṛdika is considered his son.
Devamīḍha, Śatadhanu, and Kṛtavarman were his sons.
The wife of the heroic Devamīḍha was named Māriṣā;
in her he begot ten sinless sons:
Vasudeva, Devabhāga, Devaśravas, and Ānaka.
At his birth, celestial kettledrums and drums resounded for Sṛñjaya, Śyāmaka, Kaṅka, Śamīka, Vatsaka, and Vṛka;
they call Vasudeva the abode of Hari, Ānakadundubhi.
Pṛthā, Śrutadevā, Śrutakīrti, Śrutaśravā,
and Rājādhidevī were their five sisters;
for Śūra, the father of Kunti’s friend, gave Pṛthā to him as he was childless.
Having propitiated Durvāsas, she received from him the *vidyā* known as Devahūtī.
To test its power, the pure woman summoned the Sun;
seeing the god arrive at that very moment, her mind was filled with wonder.
"O Goddess, I employed you for the sake of gaining confidence; please forgive me.
I shall bestow upon you a son who will ensure that the sight of the Lord is not in vain, and I shall act so that your womb is not defiled, O slender-waisted one."
Having thus deposited the embryo within her, the Sun departed for heaven;
immediately, a boy was born who was like a second sun.
Fearing the world, she cast him into the waters of the river with great difficulty.
Her great-grandfather Pāṇḍu, whose valor was truth, married her;
and Vṛddhaśarmā, the king of the Kārūṣas, took Śrutadevā as his wife,
in whom was born Dantavakra, the son of Diti who had been cursed by a sage.
Dhṛṣṭaketu, the son of Kaikeya, obtained Śrutakīrti;
from her were born five sons, the Kaikeyas, beginning with Santardana.
From Rājādhidevī were born two sons of Avanti, Jayasena and Ajātaśatru.
Damaghoṣa, the king of Cedi, took Śrutaśravas as his wife;
her son was Śiśupāla, whose birth has been described. To Devabhāga, by Kaṃsā, were born Citraketu and Bṛhadbala.
From Devaśravas, by Kaṃsavatī, were born Suvīra and Iṣumān;
likewise, from Kaṅka, by Kaṅkā, were born Baka, Satyajit, and Purujit.
Furthermore, from Rāṣṭrapālī were born Sṛñjaya, Vṛṣa, Durmarṣaṇa, and others.
Harikeśa and Hiraṇyākṣa were born from Śūrabhūmi; and Śyāmaka was born from the Apsaras Miśrakeśī.
Furthermore, Vṛka begot Vatsaka, Takṣa, Puṣkara, Śāla, and others upon Durvākṣī.
From Samīka were born Sumitrā, Arjunī, Pālā, and others;
from Sudāman was born Ānaka; and from Karṇikā were born Ṛtadhāmā and Ajayā.
Furthermore, [the daughters of Vajra were] Pauravī, Rohiṇī, Bhadrā, Madirā, Rocanā, and Ilā.
Devakī and others were the wives of Ānakadundubhi;
from them were born Balarāma, Gada, Sāraṇa, Durmada, Vipula, and Dhruva.
Vasudeva, however, begot Kṛta and the others by Rohiṇī.
Subhadra, Bhadrabāhu, Durmada, and Bhadra— these were the twelve sons of Pauravī, beginning with Bhūta. Nanda, Upananda, Kṛtaka, Śūra, and others were the sons of Madirā.
Kauśalyā gave birth to Keśin alone, the delighter of his lineage;
from Rocanā were born Hastin, Hemāṅgada, and others;
and from Ilā he begot Uruvalka and other principal sons of the Yadu line.
Vipṛṣṭha was born of Dhṛtadevā to Ānakadundubhi; O King, Śāntideva’s sons were Praśama, Prasita, and others;
and there were ten sons of Upadevā, beginning with Rājanya and Kalpavarṣa.
Vasuhā, Haṃsa, Suvamśa, and others were the six sons of Śrīdevā;
furthermore, nine sons beginning with Gada were obtained by her from Devarakṣitā. Vasudeva begot eight sons by Sahadevā.

Vasudeva, of noble intellect, begot eight sons upon Devakī who were like Dharma himself manifesting as the Vasus— the foremost among those renowned for their sacred learning: Kīrtimān, Suṣeṇa, and Bhadrasena.
Ṛju, Sammardana, Bhadra, and Saṅkarṣaṇa were the lords of the earth;
the eighth among them was indeed Hari himself.
And Subhadrā, O King, the highly fortunate one, was your grandmother.
Whenever there is a decline of dharma and an increase of evil,
then the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, manifests Himself;
for there is no cause for His birth, O King, other than [the state of] karma.
The illusory activity of the Supreme Person— the witness and Self of all—
which brings about the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the world, is intended as a grace for the cessation of that illusion and for the attainment of the Self.
He made an effort to relieve the burden of the earth, which was being oppressed by the lords of the *akṣauhiṇīs*— the asuras who bore the marks of kings—
deeds that were immeasurable even to the minds of the lords of the gods.

Together with Saṅkarṣaṇa, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana performed that most meritorious and glorious act which dispels the suffering, grief, and darkness of those who will be born in the Kali age, out of his grace toward his devotees.
In that supreme sacred field of glory, which is nectar for the ears, one who sips even once with the cupped hands of the ears shakes off the latent impressions of karma;
[a land] filled with the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Madhus, Śūrasenas, and Daśārhas.
With his praiseworthy deeds constantly celebrated by the Kurus, Sṛñjayas, and Pāṇḍavas; with his noble glances accompanied by affectionate smiles and his words;
with his playful prowess and his form beautiful in every limb, he delighted the world of men.

Whose face—with its shark-shaped earrings adorning his ears, his beautiful cheeks radiant with playful smiles—was a perpetual festival; drinking it in with their eyes, women and men were filled with joy, while the gods, even when angry, could not look away.
Born, he departed from his father’s house to prosper the Vraja; having slain his enemies, he performed noble deeds and produced hundreds of sons.
Having begotten them, the Supreme Person performed sacrifices among them, proclaiming to the people his own nature as revealed in the Vedas.

Indeed, lightening the heavy burden of the earth by means of the internal strife of the Kurus—the Kali age arising from within—he dispersed the armies of kings with his glance; having proclaimed victory in the conquest and having instructed Uddhava regarding the supreme truth, he departed for his own abode.
